2 marks: Predicts that the speed at the bottom increases, with a partial explanation of why
1 mark: Provides a relevant prediction without an explanation
markerNotes: The prediction must state the direction of the change, not just that the trolley is different.
Trace the chain from a higher release height to more gravitational potential energy, then to kinetic energy at the bottom.
A prediction with no reason is at most a 1-mark answer.
commonStudentErrors: Predicts the trolley will be slower at the bottom, because it has further to travel.
Explains the change in speed by saying the trolley is heavier, although its mass has not changed.
Gives an energy reason but never states whether the speed increases or decreases.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model predicts that the trolley will reach a greater speed at the bottom of the ramp. A higher release height gives the trolley more gravitational potential energy, which is the cause. On a smooth ramp, conservation of energy means this energy converts to kinetic energy as the trolley descends, so a greater kinetic energy at the bottom means a greater speed, which is the effect. This cause-and-effect relationship is the basis of the prediction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the direction of the change is stated, and the energy link runs from release height to kinetic energy at the bottom. The 2-mark answer predicts the change but gives only a vague reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: The trolley will be faster at the bottom because it starts higher, so it has more energy that turns into speed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: the prediction is correct and the reason is partial. Naming gravitational potential energy and its conversion to kinetic energy would lift it to full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The trolley will be faster at the bottom of the ramp.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: a correct prediction with no reasoning. Explaining why the speed changes would raise it.

prompts.question: Assess the usefulness of this model for predicting braking distance. Use a cause-and-effect relationship to support your judgement, and include at least one limitation of the model.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student builds a simple model that predicts the braking distance of a car from its speed. The model assumes the braking force from the road is the same at every speed, and it does not include the driver's reaction time. The model has been tested only on a dry, level road.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the usefulness of the model, using a sustained cause-and-effect chain from speed to kinetic energy to braking distance, and a specific limitation weighed against its value
5 marks: Assesses the usefulness of the model, with a clear cause-and-effect link and a relevant limitation
4 marks: Assesses the model with a relevant cause-and-effect link, but the limitation is general or missing
3 marks: Describes the model and a relevant cause-and-effect link, without a judgement
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the model, with some relevant reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about braking
markerNotes: A judgement of usefulness must be stated, not implied by describing the model.
Tie each limitation to a specific effect on the predicted braking distance.
Set out the chain in order: speed, kinetic energy, work done by the brakes, distance travelled.
commonStudentErrors: States the model is accurate because it gives a sensible answer, with no limitation.
Lists limitations with no link to the predicted braking distance.
Describes the model without making any judgement of how useful it is.

sampleAnswers.answer: Simple modelling of this kind is useful for predicting the general trend in braking distance. A faster car has more kinetic energy, so with the same braking force from the road, the brakes must do more work to remove that energy before the car stops. This cause-and-effect relationship means the braking distance increases with speed, and the model captures this trend well. The model is therefore a valuable tool for showing drivers and designers the risk of higher speeds. However, a key limitation is that the model assumes the braking force is constant. On a wet road the friction force is lower, so the real braking distance would be longer than the model predicts. The model also ignores the driver's reaction time, which adds distance before the brakes are applied. It is useful as a qualitative prediction, but its assumptions limit how far its predictions can be trusted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a sustained judgement of usefulness, builds a clear cause-and-effect chain, and weighs a specific limitation against the model's value. The 3-mark answer describes the trend but makes no judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model shows that braking distance increases with speed. A faster car has more kinetic energy, so the brakes must do more work to stop it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: the model and its energy link are described, but there is no judgement and no limitation. Adding a judgement of usefulness would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model assumes a constant braking force from the road.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with one relevant feature of the model. It gives no judgement and no cause-and-effect reasoning.

dotPoints.description: Evaluate and modify a scientific investigation in response to new evidence

prompts.question: Describe one change to the method that the class should make to test whether friction explains the lower accelerations.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class investigates how the angle of a ramp affects the acceleration of a trolley. Their first trial shows acceleration increasing with angle, but the acceleration at each angle is consistently lower than the class expected. A group member notices that the wheels were dusty and that the trolley did not run freely on the track.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes a specific change to the method, linked to how it tests friction as the cause of the lower accelerations
2 marks: Describes a change to the method that would reduce friction
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of the set-up, such as the dusty wheels
markerNotes: Name one specific change, such as cleaning the wheels, rather than a general improvement like 'be more careful'.
Say what the change tests: whether friction, rather than the ramp angle, causes the lower accelerations.
Keep the other conditions controlled so that the change is the only difference between trials.
commonStudentErrors: Suggests repeating the trials without changing anything, so the same result is expected.
Proposes a general change, such as 'use better equipment', with no link to friction.
Changes the ramp angle range instead of testing the friction explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class should modify the method by cleaning the wheels and track, then repeating the trials at every angle. This responds to the new evidence, and keeping the release point as a controlled variable means any change in acceleration can be attributed to reduced friction. If friction explains the lower results, the cleaned trolley should accelerate closer to the expected value at each angle, which supports the conclusion of this scientific investigation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: one specific change is described, with a link to testing friction as the cause. The 2-mark answer names a change but does not say what result would support the friction explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class should clean the wheels and track, then repeat the trials. This will show whether friction was the cause.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing a change that reduces friction. Saying what result would support the friction explanation would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wheels were dusty.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a relevant feature of the set-up. It does not describe a change.

prompts.question: Recommend one modification to the investigation that would test whether air resistance explains the remaining difference at steep angles. Justify your recommendation using the new evidence.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: After cleaning the wheels and track, the class's trolley accelerates close to the expected value at small ramp angles, but the acceleration at steep angles is still noticeably lower than expected. The trolley reaches its highest speeds on the steepest ramp, and the class has no data on how the trolley's shape affects its motion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Recommends a specific modification that tests air resistance, justified by the pattern in the new evidence and the speeds reached on steep ramps
5 marks: Recommends a relevant modification that tests air resistance, with a justification linked to the new evidence
4 marks: Recommends a relevant modification, with a partial justification
3 marks: Describes a relevant modification without a clear justification
2 marks: Identifies a relevant factor, such as air resistance, with little reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the investigation
markerNotes: The recommendation must be one specific change that isolates air resistance, such as a streamlined trolley on the same ramp angles.
The justification must cite the pattern in the new evidence, not just the general idea of air resistance.
Say what result would support air resistance as the cause, and what result would point back to friction.
commonStudentErrors: Recommends repeating the same trials with the same trolley, which cannot test air resistance.
Gives a justification that is not linked to the new evidence at steep angles.
Recommends changing the range of ramp angles without a link to air resistance.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class should modify the investigation by repeating the steep-angle trials with a streamlined trolley, keeping the ramp, release point and track as controlled variables. The new evidence shows the largest gap in acceleration at steep angles, where the trolley reaches its highest speeds. Air resistance increases with speed and opposes motion, so it would take more energy from the trolley at those angles. If the gap shrinks for the streamlined trolley, air resistance is supported as the cause, whereas a gap that stays the same would point back to friction. This comparison of two trolleys is a fair test within this scientific investigation. The class should repeat each angle several times with each trolley, so that random variation is not mistaken for a real difference between the shapes. Comparing the acceleration at each angle, rather than only the final speed, shows whether the gap grows with angle as air resistance predicts. Recording the room temperature and checking both trolleys' wheels and track before each run keeps the other conditions controlled.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Recommends one specific change that isolates air resistance and justifies it with the pattern in the new evidence. The 3-mark answer names a change without any justification.

sampleAnswers.answer: The class could repeat the trials with a streamlined trolley on the same ramp angles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: a relevant modification is described without a clear justification. Linking it to the larger gap at steep angles would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The trolley's shape may affect air resistance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with relevant information about the trolley. It does not recommend a change.

dotPoints.description: Explain why current scientific knowledge is both contestable and testable by further inquiry

prompts.question: Explain why the long success of Newton's laws does not put them beyond challenge, and how further inquiry could test them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student argues that Newton's laws of motion are settled, because they have described everyday motion accurately for centuries. A classmate points out that Einstein's theory of relativity refined Newton's laws for objects moving at speeds close to the speed of light and in very strong gravitational fields.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the knowledge is contestable because predictions can fail, and testable through further inquiry, with a specific example
2 marks: Explains that the knowledge can be challenged or tested, with a partial reason
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of Newton's laws, such as their predictive success
markerNotes: Explain both halves: why the knowledge can be challenged and why it can be tested, rather than one of these alone.
Use the relativity example to show that a model can be refined, not simply thrown out.
Link testability to predictions that can be checked by further inquiry.
commonStudentErrors: Says Newton's laws are proven true, so they can never be challenged.
Says the laws are wrong because relativity exists, with no explanation of the refinement.
Explains only that scientists can test the laws, not why they can be challenged.

sampleAnswers.answer: Newton's laws are contestable because any model can be challenged when its predictions fail to match observations. Relativity showed that they are an approximation at very high speeds and in strong gravity, so they were refined rather than proven complete. They are testable because their predictions can be checked by further inquiry, such as experiments that measure motion at extreme speeds. Scientific knowledge therefore stays open to revision as new evidence arrives.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both contestable and testable are explained, with the relativity example showing refinement and a clear link to further inquiry. The 2-mark answer gives a partial reason without explaining how the laws are tested.

sampleAnswers.answer: Newton's laws could be wrong, because scientists can test them with new experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: the knowledge is open to challenge or testing, with a partial reason. Explaining the relativity refinement would lift it to full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Newton's laws predicted everyday motion accurately for centuries.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a relevant feature of the laws. It does not explain why they are open to challenge or testing.

prompts.question: Discuss why scientists continue to test a well-supported model, such as the particle model of matter, and why that model may still change.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A science teacher tells her Year 11 class that the particle model of matter is well supported by evidence. A student asks why scientists still test a model that already works well for everyday experiments.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses why the model is both testable and contestable, using a specific example of new evidence and how revised models build on earlier ones
4 marks: Discusses why the model is testable and may change, with a relevant example
3 marks: Describes how the model can be tested, with some reference to change
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the model, with some relevant reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about scientific models
markerNotes: Discuss both sides: why a well-supported model is still testable, and why it may be contestable.
Use an example of evidence or a limit of the particle model, rather than general claims about science.
Show how a revised model keeps what works and replaces what fails.
commonStudentErrors: Says the particle model is proven true because it works for everyday experiments.
Says scientists test models only to check whether they are wrong, with no reference to further inquiry.
Describes the particle model without discussing why it may change.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scientists keep testing a well-supported model because scientific knowledge is testable. A model that works for everyday experiments still makes predictions, and each new test either strengthens it or reveals a limit. The particle model explains the states of matter and the behaviour of gases, but it is a simplified picture, so new evidence can show where it is incomplete. This makes the model contestable, since a clear failure can prompt a revision. Further inquiry is valuable because it can extend the model to new conditions, such as very high temperatures or very small scales. The model may therefore change, but this does not mean it was wrong. Revised models keep what predicts well and replace what fails, so scientific knowledge becomes more reliable over time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses both testability and contestability with a specific example, and shows how revised models build on earlier ones. The 3-mark answer describes testing but gives no example of change.

sampleAnswers.answer: A model can be tested by checking its predictions, and new evidence can show that it needs to change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes testing and briefly mentions change. Discussing why the model may change, with an example, would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The particle model describes matter as made of particles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about models. It does not discuss testing or change.

dotPoints.description: Construct evidence-based arguments and recognise the role of peer review in the evaluation of scientific practices, solutions or conclusions

prompts.question: Outline how peer review could help check the group's conclusion before the bulletin publishes it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A group of students concludes that a new lubricant reduces the friction on their trolley track. Before the conclusion is printed in the school science bulletin, a teacher asks other students to check the data and the method.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how peer review checks the evidence, method and conclusion before publication, and how the feedback strengthens the evidence-based argument
2 marks: Outlines that peer review involves other people checking the conclusion before it is shared
1 mark: Identifies a relevant feature of the conclusion, such as the claim about friction
markerNotes: Describe what reviewers check: the data, the method and whether the conclusion follows from them.
Explain the effect of review: errors or unsupported claims can be found and revised before publication.
Treat peer review as a process of evaluation, not just a comment from a friend.
commonStudentErrors: Says peer review means the group checks its own conclusion before publishing.
Describes peer review as proving the conclusion is correct.
Describes the lubricant instead of how the conclusion would be checked.

sampleAnswers.answer: Peer review is the assessment of a conclusion by other people with relevant knowledge before it is published. Reviewers check whether the data support the claim that the lubricant reduces friction, and whether the method was controlled and repeated. Their feedback can strengthen the evidence-based argument or show where more evidence is needed before the bulletin prints it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: explains what reviewers check and how the feedback strengthens the evidence-based argument. The 2-mark answer says others check the conclusion but does not say what they check.

sampleAnswers.answer: A classmate checks the group's conclusion and the data before it is shared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: names other people checking the conclusion before it is shared. Saying what reviewers check, such as the data and method, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The group claims the lubricant reduces friction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the group's claim. It does not explain how peer review works.

prompts.question: Construct an evidence-based argument for whether the group's conclusion that the lubricant reduces friction is supported. Refer to the strengths and weaknesses of their data.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The group's data show that trolleys on the treated track reach a higher speed at the end of the track than trolleys on the untreated track. The group ran five trials on each track, did not record the room temperature, and did not check the cleanliness of the track before the trials.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a sustained evidence-based argument that weighs the strengths and weaknesses of the data and reaches a supported judgement on the conclusion
5 marks: Constructs an evidence-based argument, weighing the data and reaching a judgement on the conclusion
4 marks: Constructs a relevant argument from the data, with some reference to a weakness
3 marks: Describes the data and a conclusion, with limited reasoning about its reliability
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the trials, with little reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the investigation
markerNotes: Build the argument in steps: state a claim, support it with specific data, then weigh the weaknesses that limit how far the claim can go.
Name specific weaknesses, such as five trials, the unrecorded temperature and a dusty track, rather than saying the data are 'not good enough'.
A supported judgement can conclude the claim is possible but not yet proven.
commonStudentErrors: Says the conclusion is correct because the treated trolleys were faster, with no weakness discussed.
Lists weaknesses without linking them to whether the conclusion is supported.
Says the data are unreliable without naming any specific weakness.

sampleAnswers.answer: The data support the conclusion only partly. The data have a clear strength, a consistent pattern, but several weaknesses. The treated trolleys reached a higher speed at the end of the track, which is consistent with less friction, so the claim is a reasonable hypothesis. However, this evidence-based argument has a weakness: five trials on each track is a small sample, so random variation could explain the difference. The room temperature was not recorded, and temperature can change the properties of the lubricant and the track, so the comparison is not fully controlled. The track was not checked for cleanliness, and dust could increase friction on the untreated track. A stronger test would repeat the trials, record the conditions and check the surfaces before each run. Peer review would be valuable here, because other students could identify these weaknesses before the conclusion is shared. Overall, the data suggest the lubricant may reduce friction, but the conclusion is not yet supported.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a sustained argument weighs the data's strengths and weaknesses and reaches a supported judgement. The 3-mark answer draws the conclusion from speed alone and mentions only one weakness.

sampleAnswers.answer: The treated trolleys reached a higher speed, so the lubricant seems to reduce friction. The group did not record the temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes the data and a conclusion, with limited reasoning about reliability. Linking the weaknesses to whether the claim is supported would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The group ran five trials on each track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the trials. It does not construct an argument.

dotPoints.description: Select and use appropriate digital, visual, written and oral media to convey scientific arguments

prompts.question: Describe which medium the student should use to present the trend to Year 8 students at the assembly, and explain why it suits the audience and time limit.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has found a clear trend in a classmate's stopping-distance data, and she needs to present it to Year 8 students at a school assembly. She has three minutes to speak and must choose the medium that best conveys the scientific argument.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes an oral and visual medium that suits the audience and time limit, with a reason linked to how the trend is conveyed
2 marks: Describes a suitable medium for the audience, with limited reasoning
1 mark: Identifies a medium that could be used, such as a graph or a slideshow
markerNotes: Choose a medium and say why it suits both the audience and the time limit.
Link the medium to what it shows: the trend is clearest in a graph, while the argument is explained aloud.
Name the medium specifically, such as a line graph or a short digital slideshow, not just 'technology'.
commonStudentErrors: Picks a written report for a live assembly, which the students will not read in three minutes.
Names a medium without saying why it suits the audience.
Chooses a video of the trials that is too long for the three-minute limit.

sampleAnswers.answer: An oral presentation with a simple visual, such as a line graph, is the best medium for these students and fits the time limit. It suits the audience because the graph shows the trend at a glance while the speaker explains the scientific argument aloud. A digital slideshow of two or three slides could support the talk, but a written report would not hold attention at an assembly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: names an oral and visual medium, fitted to the audience and time, and links it to how the trend is conveyed. The 2-mark answer names a suitable medium with only limited reasoning.

sampleAnswers.answer: An oral presentation suits Year 8 students, who need the trend explained simply.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing a suitable medium for the audience. Adding why it fits the three-minute limit would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A line graph could show the trend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a medium. It does not explain how it suits the audience.

prompts.question: Justify the combination of media she should use for this panel. Your answer should explain how each medium conveys part of the scientific argument.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The same student must present her full investigation of stopping distance to a panel of local engineers and scientists, with a 10-minute talk followed by questions. She must also give the panel a written summary of her data, and she has a line graph, a short video of the trials and a table of measurements.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a combination of media for the panel, linking each medium to a specific part of the scientific argument and the needs of the audience
5 marks: Justifies a suitable combination of media, with a link to the audience
4 marks: Justifies a combination of media, with limited links to the audience
3 marks: Describes two suitable media for the panel, without a justification
2 marks: Identifies a medium that suits the panel, with little reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the media available
markerNotes: Justify the combination, not each medium alone: say why the media work together for this panel.
Tie each medium to a part of the scientific argument, such as the trend, the method or the data.
Consider the audience: a panel of specialists will check the evidence, so precision and checkability matter.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the three media without saying what each one conveys.
Chooses a long video of the trials, which a 10-minute talk cannot fit alongside questions.
Ignores the written summary the panel expects to receive.

sampleAnswers.answer: Her combination should be an oral presentation supported by visuals and a written summary. The ten-minute talk lets her explain the scientific argument in her own words, which suits a panel that will ask questions. The line graph is the strongest visual, because it shows the trend in stopping distance against speed clearly, but she should label the axes and state the units so the audience can read it unaided. The short video of the trials is useful evidence of how the data were collected, but it should be brief, since the panel will judge the method rather than watch a long recording. The written summary gives the panel a permanent record of the measurements and method that engineers will want to check. A digital copy of the slides and summary would also let the panel review the evidence after the session. Together, the media convey the argument through explanation, visual trend and checkable detail.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies the combination by linking each medium to part of the argument and to the panel's need to check the evidence. The 3-mark answer lists media without any justification.

sampleAnswers.answer: She could use a line graph, a video and an oral presentation for the panel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes suitable media without a justification. Explaining what each medium conveys would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The video of the trials shows how the data were collected.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the trial video. It does not justify a combination of media.

dotPoints.description: Apply appropriate scientific notations, language and nomenclature

prompts.question: Outline two corrections the student should make to the notation or nomenclature in this report.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's lab report contains the sentences 'The trolley weighed 0.5 Kg' and 'The acceleration was 3 m/sec2 down the ramp'. The teacher will not mark the report until its scientific notation and nomenclature are corrected.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines two corrections, each identifying the notation or nomenclature error and giving the appropriate SI symbol or term
2 marks: Outlines one correction to the notation, language or nomenclature
1 mark: Identifies a notation or nomenclature error in the report
markerNotes: Name each error and give its correction, such as the SI symbol kg, or the term mass in place of weight.
Mass is measured in kilograms and weight is a force measured in newtons, so the two terms must not be used interchangeably.
Write symbols in their exact SI form, not as casual abbreviations.
commonStudentErrors: Says the unit should be written in full as kilograms, with no correction to the symbol.
Replaces the mass with a force in newtons, which changes the meaning rather than the notation.
Identifies the units as wrong but does not say how to write them.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should write the mass as 0.5 kg, not 0.5 Kg, because the SI unit symbol for kilogram has a lowercase k. The report should also say the trolley has a mass of 0.5 kg, not that it weighed 0.5 kg, because mass is measured in kilograms while weight is a force measured in newtons. Using the correct symbol and term in each case follows the scientific notation and nomenclature the audience expects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: two corrections, each naming the error and giving the SI symbol or correct term. The 2-mark answer gives only the symbol correction.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should write kg, not Kg, because the SI unit symbol for kilogram is lowercase.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row with one correct notation correction. Adding the mass and weight correction would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The report uses Kg, which is not the correct symbol.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a notation error. It does not give a correction.

prompts.question: Assess how well this conclusion uses scientific language, notation and nomenclature for a specialist audience. Refer to at least two changes that would improve it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's conclusion reads: 'The trolley goes faster down the steeper ramp cos it has more energy. The KE goes up and the speed is bigger, and the data is good so the friction was low.' The conclusion will be read by a panel of Year 12 physics students, who expect precise terms, symbols and units.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the conclusion's scientific language, notation and nomenclature for a specialist audience, with at least two specific changes that improve precision
5 marks: Assesses the conclusion's language and notation, with a specific change that improves precision
4 marks: Assesses the conclusion's language, with some reference to the audience
3 marks: Describes a feature of the language or notation, without a judgement
2 marks: Identifies an informal term in the conclusion
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the conclusion
markerNotes: Judge the conclusion against its audience: a panel of physics students expects defined symbols, precise terms and units.
Name specific changes, such as defining KE as kinetic energy or replacing 'cos' with a formal connective.
Separate informal wording from imprecise terms, since both affect how well the argument can be checked.
commonStudentErrors: Calls the whole conclusion poorly written without naming any specific term or symbol.
Says KE is wrong, when the problem is that it is not defined for the audience.
Assesses only the grammar and ignores the missing units and undefined symbol.

sampleAnswers.answer: The conclusion uses some scientific language, but it is informal and imprecise for a specialist audience. The word 'cos' is a casual abbreviation, and 'the trolley goes faster' should use speed, stating the direction of motion where it matters. The symbol KE is used without being defined, so the panel cannot be sure it means kinetic energy, and the term should be written in full on first use. The phrase 'the data is good' is vague and gives no evidence for the claim, so the student should cite specific measurements and their uncertainty. The nomenclature is also loose, since 'the friction was low' does not say how low, or compared with what. Using correct scientific notation, with units and defined symbols, would make the conclusion easier for the panel to check, so the student should state the unit for each speed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the conclusion's language and notation against the panel's needs and names specific changes that improve precision. The 3-mark answer describes informal wording and an undefined symbol, but makes no judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The conclusion uses informal wording, such as 'cos', and the symbol KE is not defined.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing features of the language and symbols. Judging how these affect the panel, with specific changes, would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The conclusion uses the word cos, which is informal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row with a relevant point about the conclusion. It does not assess the language or suggest changes.

dotPoints.description: Use evidence and correct scientific language and terminology to address a specific audience and purpose in a variety of contexts

prompts.question: Demonstrate how the group could explain its trolley result to a Year 7 class, using one piece of evidence and correct scientific terminology.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A group found that a trolley travelled further on a smooth track than on a rough track when pushed with the same force. The group must explain this result to a Year 7 class in one minute, and its purpose is to help the students understand friction.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates a clear explanation for the audience, using one piece of evidence and correct scientific terminology for the purpose
2 marks: Explains the trolley result for the audience, with some correct terminology
1 mark: Identifies a relevant piece of evidence from the investigation
markerNotes: Show the audience a concrete example: one piece of evidence, explained in terms they can follow.
Use the correct term, friction, with a short definition, rather than a casual word such as 'grip'.
State the purpose of the explanation so the response is clearly aimed at Year 7 students.
commonStudentErrors: Gives a full list of every measurement, which is too much for a one-minute explanation.
Uses casual words such as 'grip' or 'stickiness' without the term friction.
Explains friction with technical terms, such as coefficients, that a Year 7 audience has not met.

sampleAnswers.answer: For this Year 7 audience, the purpose is to show that friction slows a moving object. The evidence is that the trolley travelled further on the smooth track than on the rough track when pushed with the same force. Using scientific terminology, the group can say that the rough surface produces more friction between the wheels and the track, which removes more kinetic energy, so the trolley stops sooner.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: a clear explanation for the audience, using one piece of evidence and correct terminology for the purpose. The 2-mark answer explains the result with some correct terms but does not cite the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Friction slows the trolley down on the rough track, so it travels a shorter distance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining the result with some correct terminology. Adding the specific evidence from the investigation would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The trolley travelled a shorter distance on the rough track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying a relevant piece of evidence. It does not explain the result for the audience.

prompts.question: Analyse how the group should adapt its use of evidence and scientific terminology for each of these two audiences and purposes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The same group must communicate its friction result in two contexts: a one-minute talk to a Year 7 class, and a formal written report for science competition judges, who are scientists and teachers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the evidence and terminology change for each audience and purpose, with specific adaptations that show why each suits its context
5 marks: Analyses the adaptation of evidence and terminology for both audiences, with a specific reason for each
4 marks: Analyses the use of evidence for both audiences, with some reference to terminology
3 marks: Describes the evidence for one audience, without a clear adaptation for the other
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the evidence, with little reference to the audience
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the group's result
markerNotes: Analyse the same evidence twice: say what changes for each audience and why, rather than describing the two contexts separately.
Match the terminology to the audience: everyday words for Year 7 and defined technical terms for the judges.
Name a specific adaptation, such as one piece of evidence for the talk and a full method for the report.
commonStudentErrors: Uses the same report-level detail for the one-minute talk to Year 7 students.
Describes the two contexts without saying what changes between them.
Uses technical terms in the talk without defining them for a Year 7 audience.

sampleAnswers.answer: For the Year 7 class, the group's purpose is to build understanding, so its evidence should be simple and concrete. It should compare the trolley's distance on the smooth and rough tracks, using everyday language such as 'friction slows things down', with the scientific term friction defined in one sentence. The talk lasts one minute, so one piece of evidence is enough. For the competition judges, the purpose is to persuade a critical audience that the result is valid, so the written report needs precise scientific terminology, complete data and a clear method. It should define friction as a contact force opposing motion, state the number of trials and the conditions, and discuss the variables that could affect the result. The same evidence therefore appears in both contexts, but the language, detail and structure must change to suit each audience and purpose.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses how the evidence and terminology change for each audience and purpose, with specific adaptations that show why each suits its context. The 3-mark answer describes the talk but says nothing about the report.

sampleAnswers.answer: For the Year 7 class, the group should use the trolley distances in a short talk and explain friction in everyday words.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the evidence for the Year 7 talk only. Analysing how the report would differ would lift it to the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The trolley travelled further on the smooth track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the result. It does not analyse the two audiences.

dotPoints.description: Classify distance, displacement, time, speed, velocity and acceleration as either scalar or vector quantities

prompts.question: Classify the cyclist's distance travelled, her displacement and the time taken for the trip as scalar or vector quantities, and explain the feature that separates them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A cyclist rides 3 km due east along a straight bike path from her home to a cafe. The trip takes a few minutes, and a student records the distance, the displacement and the time for the trip.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies distance and time as scalars and displacement as a vector, and explains that displacement includes direction as well as magnitude
2 marks: Classifies distance, displacement and time correctly, without explaining the feature that separates them
1 mark: Classifies one of the quantities correctly
markerNotes: Name direction as the feature that separates a vector from a scalar, rather than saying displacement is simply the more important measure.
Keep time and distance in the scalar group, since each has a size but no direction.
Refer to the cyclist's trip so the classification is tied to the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Says displacement is a scalar because it is measured in kilometres, the same unit as distance.
Classifies distance as a vector because the cyclist moved along the path.
Classifies all three quantities as vectors because they all describe the trip.

sampleAnswers.answer: Distance travelled is a scalar quantity, because it has magnitude only: the 3 km length of path the cyclist covered. Displacement is a vector quantity, because it has magnitude and direction: 3 km due east from her home to the cafe. Time taken is also a scalar. The feature that separates them is direction, which displacement records and distance does not.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: distance and time are classified as scalars, displacement as a vector, and the answer names direction as the separating feature. The answer is compact and ties each classification to the trip.

sampleAnswers.answer: Distance and time are scalar quantities, and displacement is a vector quantity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by classifying all three quantities correctly. It does not explain that displacement has a direction, and adding that reason would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Distance is a scalar quantity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by classifying one quantity correctly. Classifying displacement as a vector as well would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse why the cyclist's velocity changes as she rides around the track, even though her speed stays the same, and what this shows about her acceleration.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A cyclist rides around a circular bike track. Her speedometer shows the same reading all the way round, but her direction of travel changes continuously as she follows the curve of the track.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses why velocity changes when its direction changes while speed stays constant, and links this to a non-zero acceleration
4 marks: Analyses that velocity is a vector whose direction changes, so a change in its direction means the cyclist is accelerating
3 marks: Explains that speed is a scalar that stays the same, while velocity includes direction, which changes as she rides
2 marks: Identifies that the cyclist's speed is constant, or that her velocity changes
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about speed, velocity or acceleration
markerNotes: Separate speed, which is a scalar and stays constant, from velocity, which includes direction and changes as the cyclist turns.
Link the changing velocity to acceleration, defined as the rate of change of velocity, rather than stopping at the velocity.
Use the track or the cyclist's path so the answer applies to the scenario.
commonStudentErrors: Says the cyclist has no acceleration because her speed is constant.
States that her velocity is constant because she keeps moving at the same speed.
Describes velocity as a scalar that shows how fast she is going.

sampleAnswers.answer: Speed is a scalar quantity, so it records only how fast the cyclist moves, and her speed stays steady. Velocity is a vector quantity, because it includes direction. As she rides around the track, her direction of travel changes continuously, so her velocity changes even though her speed does not. The magnitude of her velocity is her speed, which is constant, but the change in direction is enough to change the velocity vector. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so any change in velocity means she is accelerating. Her acceleration is therefore not zero, even though her speed is constant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: it analyses why velocity changes while speed stays constant and links the change to a non-zero acceleration. Each step uses the cyclist's circular path, so the answer applies to the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Her speed is a scalar that stays the same, but her velocity still changes because its direction changes as she rides round the track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that speed stays the same while velocity changes with direction. It does not analyse the acceleration this implies, which the 4- and 5-mark rows require.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cyclist is moving around a track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the cyclist's motion. It names no speed, velocity or acceleration, and identifying that her velocity changes would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use vector diagrams to represent the displacement, velocity and acceleration of an object

prompts.question: Describe how a vector diagram would represent the displacement of a bus that travels 4 km north along a straight highway, including the features that show its magnitude and direction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A bus leaves a depot and drives 4 km north along a straight highway. A transport student is asked to draw a vector diagram of the bus's displacement from the depot to its final position.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes an arrow for the displacement, with its length drawn to scale for the magnitude and its direction shown as north from the starting point
2 marks: Describes an arrow for the displacement that shows either its magnitude or its direction
1 mark: Identifies that a vector diagram uses arrows to show quantities
markerNotes: Name the two features separately: the arrow's length shows magnitude and its orientation shows direction.
Put the tail at the starting point and the tip at the final position, so the arrow shows displacement rather than the path taken.
Label the arrow and include a scale or compass direction so the diagram can be read without the text.
commonStudentErrors: Draws an arrow along the bus's path, rather than the straight line from the depot to its final position.
Draws an arrow without a direction, so only its size is shown.
Describes the arrow as showing the speed of the bus rather than its displacement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Draw a straight arrow with its tail at the depot and its tip at the bus's final position, to represent the displacement. Make the length of the arrow proportional to 4 km on a stated scale, so the magnitude is shown, and point the arrow north so the direction is shown. Label the arrow as the displacement and add a north indicator to complete the vector diagram.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by giving the tail and tip, a scaled length for the magnitude and the north direction. A middle answer would show only the direction, and a bottom answer would name the arrow without describing its features.

sampleAnswers.answer: Draw an arrow pointing north to show the bus's displacement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by showing the direction of the displacement. It does not show the magnitude, and drawing the arrow to a stated scale for 4 km would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A vector diagram uses arrows to show quantities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the arrow as the feature of a vector diagram. It does not describe how the arrow shows the displacement, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the vector diagrams for the ball's displacement, velocity and acceleration would differ at its highest point compared with a point on the way up, and explain why the acceleration arrow is the same at both points.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A ball is thrown vertically upward from the ground. It slows to rest at its highest point before falling back, and its acceleration is directed downward and stays the same throughout the flight, ignoring air resistance.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the displacement, velocity and acceleration arrows at both points, showing that velocity is zero at the top while the acceleration arrow is the same downward arrow
4 marks: Analyses how the displacement and velocity arrows differ between the two points, and identifies the acceleration as downward at both
3 marks: Compares the vector diagrams at the two points, identifying a difference in displacement or velocity
2 marks: Identifies that the ball's acceleration is directed downward throughout its flight
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the ball's motion or a vector diagram
markerNotes: Treat each quantity separately: state the length and direction of each arrow at both points.
Explain the zero velocity at the highest point in terms of the ball momentarily being at rest.
Give the reason the acceleration arrow does not change, not only that it points downward.
commonStudentErrors: Says the velocity arrow at the highest point is the longest because the ball has the greatest displacement there.
States that acceleration is zero at the highest point because the ball stops.
Draws the acceleration arrow upward on the way up, because the ball is moving upward.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the vector diagram for the highest point, the displacement arrow is drawn upward from the launch point, and it is the longest displacement arrow because the ball has risen the most. The velocity arrow has zero length, because the ball is momentarily at rest before it falls. On the way up, the displacement arrow is shorter since the ball has risen less, and the velocity arrow points upward with a non-zero length. The acceleration arrow is drawn downward at both points with the same length. This is because gravity is the only force acting, so the acceleration is constant in size and direction throughout the flight, ignoring air resistance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: it analyses the displacement, velocity and acceleration arrows at both points, shows the velocity is zero at the top, and gives the reason the acceleration arrow is unchanged.

sampleAnswers.answer: At the highest point the velocity arrow has zero length, while on the way up it points upward. The acceleration arrow still points downward at both points.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by comparing the vector diagrams at the two points and identifying a difference in velocity. It does not analyse the displacement arrows, and it does not explain why the acceleration arrow stays the same.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ball is thrown upward and falls back down.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the ball's motion. It does not draw or describe any arrow, so identifying the downward acceleration would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Add and subtract vectors in 2 dimensions

prompts.question: Outline the tip-to-tail method for finding the resultant of the drone's two displacements, one east and one north.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A drone takes off from a field, flies a straight leg due east, then turns and flies a straight leg due north. Its pilot wants a diagram showing the drone's displacement from the take-off point.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the tip-to-tail method, drawing the second vector from the tip of the first and the resultant from the tail of the first to the tip of the second
2 marks: Outlines the tip-to-tail method, without explaining how the resultant is drawn
1 mark: Identifies that vectors are added by placing them end to end
markerNotes: Place each vector tip to tail, keeping its size and direction, before drawing the resultant.
Draw the resultant from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the last, so it shows the displacement from the start point.
Name the two legs as east and north so the diagram links to the drone's flight.
commonStudentErrors: Draws the resultant from the tip of the second vector back to the start, which points the wrong way.
Adds the lengths of the two vectors and reports that total as the resultant.
Places both arrows from the same starting point and calls that the tip-to-tail method.

sampleAnswers.answer: Draw the east displacement as a vector to scale. Place the tail of the north vector at the tip of the east vector, keeping its length and direction, which is the tip-to-tail step. Draw the resultant from the tail of the east vector to the tip of the north vector. This resultant shows the drone's displacement from the take-off point.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by placing the vectors tip to tail and drawing the resultant from the first tail to the last tip. A middle answer would give the method but leave out how the resultant is drawn.

sampleAnswers.answer: Place the arrows tip to tail, so the north arrow starts where the east arrow ends.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the tip-to-tail arrangement. It does not say how the resultant is drawn, and adding that would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Vectors are added by placing them end to end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying end-to-end placement as the way vectors are added. It does not describe the steps of the method, so it does not reach the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Assess the student's claim about the direction of the change in velocity, and explain how vector subtraction gives the correct direction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A cyclist rides east at a steady speed, then turns and rides north at the same steady speed. A student claims that the change in her velocity is found by adding her initial and final velocity vectors, and that the change therefore points north-east.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the claim as incorrect, showing that subtracting the initial velocity gives a change in velocity pointing north-west, not north-east
5 marks: Assesses the claim as incorrect, explaining that adding the initial and final velocities does not give the change in velocity
4 marks: Explains that the change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, so the initial velocity is reversed before the vectors are combined
3 marks: Explains that vector subtraction is needed because velocity includes direction
2 marks: Identifies that the cyclist's velocity changes direction when she turns
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the cyclist's speed
markerNotes: Give the direction of the change in velocity, not only whether the student is right or wrong.
Show that subtracting a vector is the same as adding its reverse, so the initial east velocity points west when combined.
Draw or describe both velocity arrows from a common tail, and join the tip of the initial velocity to the tip of the final velocity.
commonStudentErrors: Says the change in velocity points north-east because it adds the two velocities.
Says the change is zero because the speed is the same.
Treats velocity as a scalar, so the directions do not affect the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is incorrect. The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, so the initial velocity must be subtracted as a vector. Subtracting a vector is the same as adding its reverse, so the eastward initial velocity is reversed to point west before it is combined with the northward final velocity. Drawing both velocities from a common tail, the change in velocity runs from the tip of the initial velocity to the tip of the final velocity, which points north-west. Adding the two velocity vectors gives a different vector that points north-east, so the student has found a sum rather than the change. The cyclist's speed is steady, but her velocity has changed because its direction has changed. Vector subtraction, not addition, therefore gives the correct direction for the change in velocity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: it assesses the claim as incorrect and shows that subtraction gives a change pointing north-west, while addition gives north-east. Each step is tied to the cyclist's turn.

sampleAnswers.answer: Velocity has direction, so the change cannot be found by adding the magnitudes. It needs vector subtraction to find the change in velocity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that vector subtraction is needed because velocity has direction. It does not show which way the change points, so it does not reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cyclist is moving at a steady speed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the cyclist's speed. It does not address the claim or the direction of the change in velocity.

dotPoints.description: Resolve vectors into components

prompts.question: Describe how to resolve a velocity vector at an angle above the horizontal into horizontal and vertical components, and state what each component represents.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A soccer ball is kicked from the ground with a velocity directed at an angle above the horizontal. A student wants to describe the ball's motion using separate horizontal and vertical parts of that velocity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the velocity as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, with the horizontal and vertical components as the two perpendicular sides, and states what each component represents
2 marks: Describes the velocity as split into horizontal and vertical parts that act at right angles
1 mark: Identifies that a vector can be split into two perpendicular parts
markerNotes: Draw the velocity as the hypotenuse, with the angle measured from the horizontal, before naming the two components.
State what each component represents: the horizontal part is the velocity along the ground and the vertical part is the velocity upward.
Say that the components act at right angles, since this is why they can be treated separately.
commonStudentErrors: Says the horizontal and vertical components add together to give the velocity.
Labels the vertical component as the side next to the angle, which mixes up the two sides.
Names the two components without saying how they are found from the velocity.

sampleAnswers.answer: To resolve the velocity vector, draw it as the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle, with its tail at the ball and the angle measured from the horizontal. The horizontal component is the side next to that angle, and it shows the velocity along the ground. The vertical component is the side opposite the angle, and it shows the velocity upward. The two components act at right angles, so each can be treated separately.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the velocity as the hypotenuse, with the horizontal and vertical components as perpendicular sides, and stating what each represents. The answer is short and keeps every step tied to the ball's velocity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The velocity splits into a horizontal part and a vertical part that act at right angles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the split into two perpendicular parts. It does not show how the parts form a right-angled triangle with the velocity, and adding that would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A vector can be split into two perpendicular parts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the split into perpendicular parts. Describing how the parts relate to the velocity, such as the triangle sides, would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Analyse how the horizontal and vertical components of the ball's velocity change as the launch angle increases from a shallow angle to a steep angle, with the launch speed held constant.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A ball is kicked from the ground at the same speed on several trials. On each trial the kicker changes the angle at which the ball leaves the ground, measured above the horizontal.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses that the horizontal component decreases and the vertical component increases as the angle rises, and links each change to how the angle sets the share of the speed along each direction
4 marks: Analyses that the horizontal component decreases and the vertical component increases as the angle increases
3 marks: Explains that the components of a velocity of fixed size depend on the angle it makes with the horizontal
2 marks: Identifies that the horizontal and vertical components act at right angles
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the ball's velocity
markerNotes: Name both components and say how each one changes, rather than describing only the horizontal part.
Link each change to the angle, because the question asks how the components respond to a change in the launch angle.
Keep the speed fixed in the answer, since the question holds the launch speed constant.
commonStudentErrors: States that the horizontal component increases with the angle, because the ball travels further.
Says the components always add up to the total velocity, rather than acting at right angles.
Says the vertical component is zero at every angle.

sampleAnswers.answer: The velocity is a vector, so to resolve it into components, the launch speed is split into a horizontal component along the ground and a vertical component upward. At a shallow angle most of the speed lies along the ground, so the horizontal component is large and the vertical component is small. As the angle increases, the velocity tilts further upward, so the horizontal component decreases and the vertical component increases. Each component depends on the angle, since the horizontal part follows the cosine of the angle and the vertical part follows the sine. With the speed held constant, the two components therefore change in opposite ways as the launch angle increases.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: it analyses both changes and links each to the angle's share of the fixed speed. The answer holds the speed constant as the question requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The vertical component gets bigger as the angle increases, because more of the ball's speed points upward.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining how one component depends on the angle. It does not describe the horizontal component, so it does not reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ball is kicked from the ground at an angle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the kick. It names no component, so identifying the horizontal and vertical parts would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Solve total distance and displacement problems
Explain how instantaneous speed, average speed, instantaneous velocity and average velocity are measured and calculated

prompts.question: Describe how the average speed and the average velocity of the trolley are each found from measurements, and explain what the velocity measurement must include that the speed measurement does not.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses a stopwatch to time a trolley as it travels along a curved path on a laboratory bench, from a starting mark to a finishing mark. She measures the length of the curved path with a tape and the straight-line distance between the two marks.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes average speed as the total distance divided by the total time, and average velocity as the displacement divided by the time, with the velocity including direction
2 marks: Describes average speed and average velocity as each found by dividing a distance or displacement by a time
1 mark: Identifies time as a measurement needed for average speed or velocity
markerNotes: Define average speed using the total distance along the path, and average velocity using the displacement from start to finish.
Name direction as the extra feature the velocity measurement needs, since the speed measurement is a scalar.
Mention the stopwatch time for both averages, because both divide by the same time interval.
commonStudentErrors: Says average velocity uses the distance along the curved path, the same as average speed.
States that average speed includes direction, because the trolley moved along a path.
Describes average speed as the time divided by the distance, reversing the ratio.

sampleAnswers.answer: Average speed is found by dividing the total distance along the curved path by the total time taken on the stopwatch. Average velocity is found by dividing the displacement, the straight-line change in position from the starting mark to the finishing mark, by the same time. The velocity measurement must include direction, which the speed measurement does not, because displacement is a vector and distance is a scalar.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: both averages are described as a distance or displacement divided by time, and the answer names direction as the extra feature of the velocity measurement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Average speed is the distance divided by the time, and average velocity is the displacement divided by the time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing both averages as a distance or displacement divided by a time. It does not say that the velocity measurement includes direction, which the 3-mark row needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both averages need the time from the stopwatch.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying time as a measurement needed. It does not say how the averages are found, so describing the division would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Distinguish between the average velocity and the average speed of a runner over one complete lap of a circular track, and explain how the instantaneous speed at the finish line can be measured.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A runner completes one full lap of a circular athletics track and finishes at the same point she started from. A school physics class wants her average speed and average velocity over the lap, and also her instantaneous speed as she crosses the finish line, which will be measured with a light gate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes average velocity from average speed using displacement and distance, explains why the average velocity is zero, and explains how a light gate gives the instantaneous speed
4 marks: Distinguishes average velocity from average speed using displacement and distance, and explains why the average velocity is zero
3 marks: Explains that average velocity depends on displacement while average speed depends on the distance travelled
2 marks: Identifies that the runner ends at her starting point, so her displacement is zero
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the lap or the runner's speed
markerNotes: Give the displacement of zero for the lap, then contrast it with the non-zero distance the runner covered.
Explain the light gate method: a very short known distance is timed, and the speed over that short distance approximates the speed at one instant.
Keep average and instantaneous measures distinct, since the question asks for both.
commonStudentErrors: Says the average velocity is not zero because the runner was moving the whole time.
States that instantaneous speed is found by dividing the lap length by the total time.
Says a light gate measures average speed over the whole lap, not the speed at one instant.

sampleAnswers.answer: Average velocity depends on displacement, the straight-line change in position from start to finish. After one complete lap the runner is back at her starting point, so her displacement is zero and her average velocity is zero. Average speed depends on distance travelled, which is the full length of the lap, so her average speed is not zero. The two averages differ because they use different measurements. A light gate measures the instantaneous speed at the finish line by timing the runner across a very short known distance. Dividing that short distance by the very short time gives a close approximation of the speed at that instant.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: it distinguishes the two averages by displacement and distance, explains why the average velocity is zero, and explains how the light gate gives the instantaneous speed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Average velocity uses displacement, and average speed uses distance. Both are divided by the time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining that average velocity depends on displacement and average speed on distance. It does not apply this to the lap, so it does not explain why the average velocity is zero.

sampleAnswers.answer: The runner goes around the track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the lap. It names no speed or velocity, so identifying the zero displacement would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Solve problems using v⃗av = Δs⃗ / Δt
Solve problems involving the calculation of velocity in 2 dimensions
Solve problems to determine speed, velocity, distance, displacement and time
Solve problems in one and 2 dimensions using a⃗ = Δv⃗ / Δt
Use data to construct displacement–time graphs, velocity–time graphs and acceleration–time graphs

prompts.question: Outline the steps a student should follow to construct a displacement–time graph from a table of time and position readings for the trolley.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses a motion sensor to record the position of a trolley every 0.5 seconds as it rolls along a straight track. The readings are entered into a table with one column for time and one column for position.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the steps to plot the graph, with time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis, labelled scales and units, each reading plotted as a point, and a smooth line drawn through the points
2 marks: Outlines the plotting of time and position readings, with some reference to axes, labels or a line through the points
1 mark: Identifies that the time and position readings are plotted on a graph
markerNotes: Name each axis by the variable it shows, with units, rather than writing only time and position.
A strong answer follows the order of the steps, from axes and scales to plotting each point and drawing the line.
Check that the scale spreads the points over most of the grid.
commonStudentErrors: Puts position on the horizontal axis and time on the vertical axis.
Joins the points with straight segments between each pair, rather than drawing one smooth line of best fit.
Leaves out the units or labels on the axes.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should draw the axes first, placing time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis. Each axis needs a suitable scale that uses most of the grid, with units and labels. Each time and position reading is then plotted as a point, and a smooth line of best fit is drawn through the points to form the displacement–time graph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the axes, scales and units, the plotting of each reading, and a smooth line through the points. A middle answer names the axes and plots the points but leaves out the scales and units.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student plots the time values on the horizontal axis and the position values on the vertical axis, then draws a line through the points.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the plotting of time and position readings, with a line through the points. The scales, units and labels are not mentioned, which the 3-mark row needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student puts the time and position readings on a graph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the readings are plotted. No axes or steps are given, so naming the axes and the plotting of each point would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.question: Construct a written plan showing how the student can use the displacement–time readings to produce a velocity–time graph and then an acceleration–time graph, naming the feature of each graph that gives the quantity for the next.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a table of position readings for a trolley taken at regular 0.5 second intervals along a straight track. The student has already plotted these readings as a displacement–time graph and now needs the velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs from the same data.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Constructs a complete plan that links each velocity to the gradient between successive readings and each acceleration to the change in velocity over time, naming the feature of each graph used for the next
5 marks: Constructs a sound plan that derives velocity from the displacement–time readings and acceleration from the velocity values, with a clear link to the gradient of each graph
4 marks: Describes how velocity is found from the displacement–time readings, and how acceleration follows from the velocity values
3 marks: Describes how velocity is found from the displacement–time data, with limited reference to acceleration
2 marks: Identifies features of the graphs, such as gradient or time intervals, with little linking between them
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the graphs
markerNotes: A complete plan names the feature used at each step: the gradient of the displacement–time graph for velocity, and the gradient of the velocity–time graph for acceleration.
Values sit at the midpoint of each time interval, which is the detail that separates a careful plan from a generic one.
State the units, metres per second and metres per second squared, so the plan can be checked.
commonStudentErrors: Says the velocity is the displacement at each reading, rather than the change in displacement over time.
Uses the height of the displacement–time graph, not its gradient, to find the velocity.
Plots the velocity values against position instead of against time.

sampleAnswers.answer: Velocity comes from the displacement–time readings. For each pair of successive readings, the change in position divided by the time interval gives the velocity, and this is plotted at the midpoint of the interval on a velocity–time graph. The feature that gives velocity is the gradient of the displacement–time graph, so each velocity equals the gradient between two readings. Acceleration then comes from the velocity–time graph in the same way. For each pair of successive velocities, the change in velocity divided by the time taken gives the acceleration, which is plotted at the midpoint of that interval on an acceleration–time graph. The feature that gives acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph. Both graphs should use the same time scale, and each value should be checked for units of metres per second and metres per second squared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: each velocity is linked to the gradient between successive readings and each acceleration to the change in velocity over time, with the feature used for each graph named. The plan is complete enough to produce both new graphs from the same readings.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student finds velocity from the gradient of the displacement–time graph, between successive readings. Acceleration is then found from the velocity values by taking the change in velocity over time. Each set of values is plotted against time on its own graph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing how velocity is found from the readings and how acceleration follows from the velocity values. It does not show the link between the gradient of each graph and the quantity plotted on the next, which the 5-mark row needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The gradient of the graph is needed for the velocity and acceleration.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying gradient as a feature, but it does not say which readings are used or how the acceleration follows. Naming the readings used for each velocity would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Use data to analyse motion graphs to describe the displacement, velocity and acceleration of an object

prompts.question: Describe the acceleration and the displacement of the trolley during the first 4 seconds, as shown by the velocity–time graph.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A trolley moves along a straight track from the origin. Its velocity–time graph is a horizontal line at a constant positive velocity from 0 to 4 seconds, and then a straight line that slopes upward from 4 to 8 seconds.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes zero acceleration from the horizontal line, and a steadily increasing positive displacement over the first 4 seconds, linked to the constant velocity
2 marks: Describes either the zero acceleration or the increasing displacement, with some reference to the graph
1 mark: Identifies that the velocity is constant over the first 4 seconds
markerNotes: Link each quantity to a feature of the graph: a zero gradient gives zero acceleration, and the area under the graph gives displacement.
Use words such as steadily increasing or positive to show direction and rate, not just increasing.
Refer to the given graph, not to motion in general.
commonStudentErrors: Says the displacement is zero because the acceleration is zero.
Reads the height of the velocity–time line as the displacement, instead of the area under it.
Describes the acceleration as non-zero because the velocity is positive.

sampleAnswers.answer: On this motion graph, the acceleration is zero over the first 4 seconds, because the velocity–time line is horizontal and its gradient is zero. The displacement is positive and increases steadily, since the trolley keeps moving forward at a constant velocity. The area under the graph over this interval gives the displacement, which is why it rises at a steady rate.
