dotPoints.description: Use magnetic field interactions to explain why a current-carrying conductor experiences a force in a magnetic field

prompts.question: EXPLAIN why a current-carrying conductor experiences a force when it is placed between the poles of a magnet, using the magnetic field interactions.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A straight wire carrying a current is placed between the poles of a horseshoe magnet, at right angles to the magnet's field.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains that the current produces a circular magnetic field around the conductor, which adds to the magnet's field on one side and opposes it on the other, so the conductor is pushed towards the weaker field
3 marks: Explains that the current's magnetic field interacts with the magnet's field, producing a net force on the conductor, without describing the stronger and weaker regions
2 marks: Identifies that the current creates a magnetic field around the conductor, without explaining how it interacts with the magnet's field
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about magnetic fields around current-carrying conductors
markerNotes: Name the field around the wire as circular, and the field of the magnet as running between the poles.
Explain where the two fields add and where they cancel, since that produces the net push.
State that the conductor moves towards the weaker field, not simply away from the magnet.
commonStudentErrors: Says the wire is pushed towards the stronger field, which reverses the explanation.
Says the force comes from the magnet alone, without mentioning the field of the current.
Says the force is caused by the current heating the wire.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current in the wire produces its own circular magnetic field around the wire. Where this field points in the same direction as the magnet's field, the two fields add, creating a region of stronger field on one side of the wire. On the opposite side, the two fields point in opposite directions and partly cancel, giving a weaker field. These magnetic field interactions push the wire out of the stronger field and towards the weaker field, so the current-carrying conductor experiences a force.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains the circular field, where the fields add and cancel, and the push towards the weaker field.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wire has a magnetic field around it when the current flows, so it is pushed by the magnet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the field around the wire, without explaining how it interacts with the magnet's field.

sampleAnswers.answer: A current-carrying wire is affected by the magnet.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: gives relevant information, with no detail on the fields.

prompts.question: DISCUSS why a current-carrying conductor placed parallel to a magnet's field experiences no net force, using the magnetic field interactions.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A straight wire carries a current and is placed so that it lies along the direction of a uniform magnetic field between two magnet poles.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses that the wire's field circles the wire at right angles to it, while the external field runs along the wire, so the field strength is the same on both sides and no net force results
4 marks: Discusses that the two fields do not reinforce on one side and oppose on the other, so there is no net force, with limited detail of the field shapes
3 marks: Describes the circular magnetic field around the wire, and states that the wire experiences no net force in this position
2 marks: Identifies that the wire is parallel to the magnetic field, without explaining the absence of force
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about magnetic fields and current-carrying conductors
markerNotes: Describe both field shapes: the wire's field circles the wire, and the external field runs along it.
Say why the field strength is the same on both sides, which is what removes the net push.
Link the answer to the rule that the force is zero when the conductor is parallel to the field.
commonStudentErrors: Says the wire is pushed towards the stronger field, as it would be at right angles.
Says the parallel wire experiences a force because it carries a current.
Says the fields cancel at every point, so the wire has no magnetic field.

sampleAnswers.answer: When the wire lies parallel to the magnet's field, the wire's own magnetic field still forms circles around the wire, perpendicular to its length. The external field from the magnet runs along the length of the wire. Because the two fields are at right angles to each other, they do not add on one side and cancel on the other. On each side of the wire, the magnetic field strength is the same, so the field lines do not push the wire sideways. These magnetic field interactions are symmetric about the wire, so there is no net force on the current-carrying conductor. This is consistent with the force on a conductor being zero when it is parallel to the uniform magnetic field.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: describes both field shapes, explains why the strengths are equal on each side, and links the result to the zero force.

sampleAnswers.answer: The current makes a circular magnetic field around the wire. Here the magnet's field runs along the wire, so the wire experiences no net force.

sampleAnswers.answer: A parallel magnetic field does not push on the wire.

prompts.question: DEDUCE the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor if both the current and the magnetic field are reversed, and explain why reversing only one of them reverses the force.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has a current-carrying conductor lying in a uniform magnetic field. The student reverses both the current and the field, then later reverses only the current.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Deduces that the force keeps its direction when both the current and the field are reversed, because the two reversals cancel, and that reversing only one of them reverses the force
4 marks: Deduces that the direction of the force is unchanged when both are reversed, with limited explanation of why reversing one reverses the force

markerNotes: Deduce from the rule that the force depends on the direction of both the current and the field.
Explain the cancelling of the two reversals, rather than only stating that the force is unchanged.

commonStudentErrors: Says reversing both the current and the field reverses the force.

sampleAnswers.answer: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field depends on the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field, so the direction of the force is determined by both. When both the current and the magnetic field are reversed, the direction of each is turned around, and the two reversals cancel. The direction of a force on the conductor is therefore the same as before, because the force depends on the combination of the current direction and the field direction, which is unchanged. Reversing only the current reverses the force, because only one of the two directions has changed. Likewise, reversing only the magnetic field reverses the force, so the force is reversed by changing either one, but not by changing both at once.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: deduces the unchanged force from the cancelling reversals, and explains that a single reversal changes the force.

sampleAnswers.answer: The magnitude of a force on a current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field is proportional to the current in the conductor and to the conductor length in the field. Increasing the current increases the number of charges moving through the field each second, so the total force on the conductor rises in proportion. Increasing the conductor length in the field increases the number of moving charges that experience the force, so the force again rises. Both changes therefore increase the magnitude of a force on the conductor.

The force also depends on the angle between the conductor and the field. When the conductor lies along the field, the angle is zero and the force is zero, since no part of the conductor is at right angles to the field. As the conductor is rotated towards right angles, the magnitude of the force increases, and it is largest when the conductor is perpendicular to the field. The change is not linear: the force follows the sine of the angle, growing most rapidly close to zero degrees and levelling off near ninety degrees.

prompts.question: ASSESS a student's laboratory experiment to demonstrate the motor effect, in which the wire is clamped and the magnet is held by hand, identifying its limitations and one improvement.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student demonstrates the motor effect by clamping a wire firmly, connecting it to a DC supply, and holding a magnet by hand near the wire. The student sees that the wire barely appears to move, and the magnet's position changes between trials.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the method by identifying that a clamped wire cannot show the motor effect and that the hand-held magnet gives an uncontrolled field, and proposes a suitable improvement with a justification
5 marks: Assesses the method by identifying two limitations, one of which is the uncontrolled field, and suggests an improvement

markerNotes: Assess the method against what the demonstration needs: a free wire and a controlled field.
Give a reason for each limitation, not just a list of faults.

sampleAnswers.answer: The main limitations of the method are that the wire is clamped, and the magnet is held by hand. The motor effect produces a force on the wire that displaces a free wire, so a clamped wire may show no visible movement even though a force acts on it. The student therefore cannot observe the demonstration. The hand-held magnet means its position, orientation and distance from the wire change between trials. The magnetic field at the wire is then neither fixed nor uniform, and it may not be at right angles to the wire, so the results cannot be compared. An improvement is to suspend a short flexible wire from a stand, fix the magnet on a stand so that the field is uniform and constant, and use an ammeter to measure the current. These changes make the laboratory experiment repeatable and show clearly that the force depends on the current and the magnetic field.

sampleAnswers.answer: Torque is the turning effect of a force about a pivot. sampleAnswers.answer: The hinges are the pivot, and the torque on the door is τ = rF sin θ, where r is the distance from the hinges to the point where the force is applied, F is the size of the force, and θ is the angle between the radius and the applied force. Torque is greater when the force is applied further from the hinges, because the radius is larger, and a larger force gives a larger torque for the same radius. Pushing close to the hinges gives a small radius, so a larger force is needed to produce the same turning effect. The angle enters through sin θ, which measures the perpendicular component of the force relative to the radius. Pushing at right angles to the door's surface gives the largest sin θ and so the greatest torque. Pushing along the door's surface towards the hinges, which is along the radius, gives zero torque. Increasing the radius or the force increases the torque, and the largest torque comes from a large force applied far from the hinges at right angles to the door.

sampleAnswers.answer: The torque on a current-carrying loop is τ = nIAB sin θ, where θ is the angle between the normal to the loop and the magnetic field. When the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field, its normal is parallel to the field, so sin θ is zero. The forces on the sides then lie in the plane of the coil and cannot turn it, so the torque is zero. When the plane is parallel to the field, the normal is at right angles to the field, so sin θ is one. The forces on opposite sides now form a couple, separated by the width of the coil, so the torque is largest.

Each turn experiences a force, so more turns increase the total force and the torque. A larger current increases the force on each current-carrying side. A larger area lengthens the sides or widens the coil, which increases the forces and their lever arm, and a stronger magnetic field increases the force on each side. The orientation of the loop is also needed, because the torque depends on sin θ, where θ is the angle between the normal to the loop and the field. sampleAnswers.answer: In a simple DC motor, the structure of the rotor coil is a loop of wire mounted on an axle, and its function is to carry the current that experiences the magnetic force. The field magnets, either permanent magnets or electromagnets, have the function of producing a magnetic field across the coil. The brushes are fixed carbon contacts that press against the rotating commutator, passing current from the supply into the coil. The split-ring commutator is a ring split into two halves, and its function is to reverse the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so that the torque keeps turning the coil in the same direction.

prompts.question: DISTINGUISH between the split-ring commutator in a simple DC motor and the slip rings in a simple AC motor, referring to how each affects the current in the rotor coil.

sampleAnswers.answer: The split-ring commutator in a DC motor is a single ring split into two halves, connected to the ends of the rotor coil, and the brushes press against it. It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so the torque keeps turning the coil in one direction. The slip rings in an AC motor are two complete rings, each permanently connected to one end of the coil, with brushes pressing on them. Slip rings do not reverse the current, so the current in the coil alternates with the supply. The AC motor's field magnets are energised by the same supply, so the field reverses in step with the coil current, keeping the torque in one direction. The commutator reverses the current mechanically, while the slip rings simply maintain the connection.

markerNotes: Judge proportionality: the question asks whether the gain is always in proportion, not whether it is positive.

sampleAnswers.answer: Adding turns to the rotor coil of a brushed electric motor does not always increase the torque in proportion, because the torque depends on the current as well as the number of turns. Each extra turn adds to the total force on the coil for a given current, so for a fixed current the torque increases with the number of turns. However, more turns mean more wire, which increases the resistance of the coil. With a fixed supply voltage, a higher resistance reduces the current through the coil. If most of the circuit's resistance is in the coil, and the resistance rises in proportion to the number of turns, the current falls by a similar proportion, and much of the gain in torque is cancelled. The extra turns also increase heating in the coil, since heat depends on the current squared and the resistance. A sound assessment concludes that more turns give some gain, but not necessarily a proportional one, and that a stronger field from the field magnets may be more effective.

sampleAnswers.answer: The electromotive force (emf) generated in a coil is proportional to the rate at which the magnetic flux through it changes, as stated by the law of electromagnetic induction and written as |ε| = N|Δϕ / Δt|. In both trials the magnet travels along the same path, so the change in magnetic flux is the same total amount. The difference is the time taken. Pushing the magnet quickly makes that change occur in a shorter time, so the change in magnetic flux per unit time is greater and the emf is larger. Pushing slowly spreads the same change over a longer time, so the change in magnetic flux per unit time is smaller and the emf is smaller. The number of turns N is the same in both trials, so it does not alter the comparison. The analysis shows that the emf depends on the change in magnetic flux per unit time, not on the total change alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Sustained analysis: it isolates the time taken as the difference, links it to the rate of flux change and the law, and states the conclusion. The middle answers reach the same idea with less reasoning.

sampleAnswers.answer: A faster push increases the rate at which the magnetic flux changes, which increases the emf given by |ε| = N|Δϕ / Δt|. A larger emf drives a larger induced current, and by Lenz's law the direction of this current is such that its magnetic field opposes the approach of the magnet. The student therefore feels a resisting force, so work done on the magnet is needed to keep it moving. The electrical energy in the circuit must come from this mechanical work. If the direction of the induced current were reversed, the magnet would be pulled into the coil by its own current, creating energy from nothing and violating the law of conservation of energy. The emf and the direction of the induced current together ensure that the work done equals the electrical energy produced, plus any thermal energy in the coil.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Sustained justification: it links the emf to the induced current, the opposing direction to the work done, and shows why reversal would break conservation.

This changing magnetic flux induces an emf in the copper. Unlike a wire, the tube is one of the conductive materials that offer many possible paths, so the induced emf drives currents round closed loops within the copper. These circulating currents are eddy currents. Their size depends on the rate at which the flux changes and on the resistance of the loops. Each eddy current produces its own magnetic field, which by Lenz's law opposes the change in flux that produced it. This opposing field pushes against the magnet, so the magnet falls more slowly than it would through a plastic tube.

sampleAnswers.answer: When the switch closes, the increasing current produces a rising magnetic flux through the solenoid's own turns. By electromagnetic induction, this change in magnetic flux induces an emf in the solenoid that opposes the change, as stated by Lenz's law. This back emf acts against the battery's emf, so the current rises gradually rather than instantly. In solenoids, the induced emf is self-induced, because it comes from the solenoid's own changing current. In straight conductors moving through a magnetic field, the emf comes instead from motion, which changes the magnetic flux through the circuit and appears across the conductor's ends. Metal plates show the same principle through eddy currents, which oppose the change in magnetic flux that produces them. The three cases are therefore all examples of one principle: an induced emf always opposes the change in magnetic flux that causes it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The doorbell circuit uses a step-down transformer, which has fewer turns on its secondary coil than on its primary coil. The primary coil is connected to the mains, and the alternating current in it produces a changing magnetic flux in the laminated soft-iron core. The core carries this flux to the secondary coil, where it induces an alternating voltage. Because the secondary coil has fewer turns, the induced voltage is less than the mains voltage, so the bell operates at a much lower voltage. Connecting the bell only to the secondary coil means it receives this reduced voltage, while the mains stays on the primary side. The structure and turns of the transformer together give it its function of reducing the voltage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by applying the step-down structure to the doorbell, with the core and both coils described accurately and the wiring explained. The middle answer describes the coils but does not apply them to the doorbell.

sampleAnswers.answer: A transformer has a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on a core. This one has fewer turns on its secondary coil, so the voltage across the bell is lower than the mains voltage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the coils and identifying the fewer secondary turns. It does not explain the function of the transformer in the doorbell circuit, so it cannot reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A transformer is used so that the bell does not run directly from the mains.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the doorbell. It does not describe the transformer's structure or how it changes the voltage.

dotPoints.description: Explain why a primary coil requires an AC input to induce an AC output in the secondary coil of a transformer

prompts.question: EXPLAIN why the voltmeter shows only a brief deflection while the battery remains connected to the primary coil.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student connects the primary coil of a transformer to a battery through a switch, and connects the secondary coil to a voltmeter. When the switch is closed, the voltmeter shows a brief deflection, and the reading then falls back to zero while the switch stays closed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the flux in the core changes only while the current is changing, so the induced voltage in the secondary coil is brief and then falls to zero
2 marks: Explains that the secondary coil needs a changing magnetic flux to produce a voltage, without linking this to the brief deflection
1 mark: Identifies that the transformer needs a changing current in the primary coil
markerNotes: Tie the brief deflection to the moment the current changes, not to the battery being connected.
Say that a steady current gives a steady flux, so the secondary voltage falls to zero.
Link the need for changing flux to why an AC input gives an AC output.
commonStudentErrors: Says the battery itself induces a voltage in the secondary coil, rather than the changing flux.
Says the voltmeter reads zero because the current is zero, when the battery current is steady but not zero.
Describes the switch closing without linking the change in current to the change in flux.

sampleAnswers.answer: The brief deflection happens because the current in the primary coil is changing as the switch closes, so the magnetic flux in the core is changing. This changing flux links the secondary coil and induces a voltage in it. Once the battery current is steady, the flux stops changing, so the induced voltage falls to zero. A transformer needs changing flux to induce a voltage, which is why an AC input would give a continuous AC output.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by linking the brief deflection to the changing current and flux, and by explaining why the steady battery current gives zero output. The middle answer explains the need for changing flux but does not relate it to the deflection.

sampleAnswers.answer: The secondary coil only produces a voltage when the magnetic flux through it changes. A battery gives a steady current, so the flux does not keep changing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by explaining the need for changing flux. It does not link this to the brief deflection, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A transformer needs a current in its primary coil to work.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that a current is needed. It gives no reason linked to the induced voltage.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY whether the student's claim is correct, referring to the magnetic flux linked with the secondary coil.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that a transformer will produce a steady output voltage from a DC supply, provided the primary coil is connected to a battery with a large enough voltage. The student's reasoning focuses only on the size of the battery's voltage.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, showing that a steady DC current gives a steady flux and therefore no induced voltage in the secondary coil
5 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, with a sound explanation of the steady flux and the induced voltage in the secondary coil
4 marks: Explains why a steady DC current gives no induced voltage, but does not clearly justify the conclusion about the claim
3 marks: Describes the magnetic flux linked with the secondary coil, with limited reasoning about the DC supply
2 marks: Identifies that a transformer needs changing flux, with minimal reference to the claim
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about transformers or DC supplies
markerNotes: State that the claim is incorrect early, then support it with the link between changing flux and induced voltage.
Explain that a larger battery voltage only gives a larger steady current, not a changing flux.
Name the switching moments as the only times a voltage appears, to show the reasoning is complete.
commonStudentErrors: Says a larger battery voltage produces a larger induced voltage in the secondary coil, which ignores the changing flux.
Accepts the claim because the transformer has coils, without referring to changing flux.
Says the secondary coil produces a voltage whenever current is flowing in the primary coil.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is incorrect. A transformer works by changing the magnetic flux in its core, and the changing flux links the secondary coil and induces a voltage in it. A DC supply from a battery gives a steady current in the primary coil once it has settled. A steady current produces a steady magnetic flux, so the flux linked with the secondary coil does not change and no voltage is induced. Making the battery's voltage larger only makes the steady current larger; it does not make the flux change. The only moments when a voltage appears are when the switch is closed or opened, because the current, and so the flux, is changing then. An AC supply keeps the current and flux changing all the time, which is why a transformer gives a continuous AC output. A steady output voltage from a DC supply is therefore not possible, and the student's reasoning overlooks the role of changing flux in induction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying that the claim is incorrect, with the steady flux and the absence of induced voltage explained. The middle answer explains the steady-flux point but does not clearly justify the conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: A transformer induces a voltage in the secondary coil from a changing magnetic flux. The battery gives a steady current in the primary coil, so the flux is steady and the induced voltage is zero. A larger battery voltage does not change this, because it only makes the steady current larger.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by explaining why a steady DC current gives no induced voltage. It does not clearly justify the conclusion about the claim, so it cannot reach the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A transformer needs a changing magnetic flux to produce a voltage in the secondary coil.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying the need for changing flux. It does not say whether the student's claim is correct or refer to the battery.

prompts.question: PREDICT whether the secondary voltage will increase, decrease or stay the same when the number of turns on the secondary coil is increased, and why.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A transformer has a primary coil connected to a fixed AC supply. In a lab experiment, the number of turns on the primary coil and the primary voltage are kept the same, but the number of turns on the secondary coil is changed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Predicts that the secondary voltage increases, and explains that the voltage ratio follows the ratio of the turns on the two coils
2 marks: Predicts that the secondary voltage increases, with a reason that refers to the turns only in general terms
1 mark: Identifies that the number of turns affects the secondary voltage
markerNotes: Predict the direction first, then give the reason from the voltage ratio: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns.
Keep the primary voltage and primary turns fixed, so the change comes only from the secondary coil.
Say the secondary voltage changes in proportion to its turns, which needs no working out.
commonStudentErrors: Says the secondary voltage stays the same because the primary voltage is unchanged.
Predicts the increase correctly but gives no reason linked to the number of turns.
Says the secondary voltage falls when more turns are added, which reverses the relationship.

sampleAnswers.answer: The secondary voltage will increase. In a transformer, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns. The primary coil keeps its voltage and number of turns, so adding turns to the secondary coil increases the ratio of secondary to primary turns, and the secondary voltage rises in the same proportion. Only the number of turns on the secondary coil changes, so it alone determines the new secondary voltage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by predicting the increase and linking it to the voltage ratio and turns ratio. The middle answer predicts the increase but gives only a general reason.

sampleAnswers.answer: The secondary voltage will increase because there are more turns on the secondary coil.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by predicting the increase with a general reason about the turns. It does not use the voltage ratio, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The number of turns changes the secondary voltage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying that the turns affect the voltage. It makes no prediction of direction.

prompts.question: ANALYSE how the relationship between the primary and secondary voltages changes, and what this means for the function of the transformer.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: An engineer replaces the secondary coil of a step-down transformer with a new coil that has more turns than the primary coil. The primary coil and the supply are left unchanged.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses the change in the turns ratio and its effect on the voltage relationship, and explains clearly that the transformer now steps up the voltage and changes function
4 marks: Analyses the change in turns and the resulting voltage relationship, with some explanation of how the function of the transformer changes
3 marks: Identifies that the secondary voltage is now greater than the primary voltage, with limited reference to the turns ratio
2 marks: Identifies the change in the number of secondary turns, without relating it to the voltages
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about transformers
markerNotes: Use Vp / Vs = Np / Ns to show the direction of the change, not only that the coil has changed.
Name the change of function explicitly: a step-down transformer becomes a step-up transformer.
Say what stays the same, so the cause of the change is clear.
commonStudentErrors: Says the transformer still steps down because the primary coil has not changed.
Describes the new coil without saying how the secondary voltage now compares with the primary voltage.
Says the secondary voltage rises but still calls the device a step-down transformer.

sampleAnswers.answer: The original step-down transformer had fewer turns on its secondary coil than on its primary coil, so its secondary voltage was less than its primary voltage. The new secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil, so the ratio of secondary turns to primary turns is now greater than one. From Vp / Vs = Np / Ns, the secondary voltage is now greater than the primary voltage, so the relationship between the two voltages has reversed. The device is now a step-up transformer, and its function has changed from reducing the voltage to increasing it. The primary coil and supply are unchanged, so the change in the number of turns on the secondary coil alone causes this reversal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing the change in turns, the reversed voltage relationship and the change in function. The middle answer identifies the reversed voltages but does not analyse the change in function.

sampleAnswers.answer: The new secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil, so the secondary voltage is now greater than the primary voltage. The transformer is no longer a step-down transformer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by identifying that the secondary voltage is now greater than the primary voltage. It gives little reference to the turns ratio, so it cannot reach the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A transformer has coils and a core, and this one has had its coil changed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about transformers. It does not relate the change to the voltages.

The energy output of both transformer A and transformer B is less than the energy input. These transformers produce heat energy in their cores due to resistive losses, magnetic effects and mechanical vibrations.
In the transmission line, heat energy is produced due to the resistance of the wires.

sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing a transformation that occurs in the transformers. It does not cover the transmission line, and naming a second transformation, such as sound from the vibrating core, would lift it to the 3-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain how the components of an AC induction motor are designed to support its function and operation

prompts.question: OUTLINE the roles of the stator and the rotor cage in turning the saw blade.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A workshop bench saw is driven by an AC induction motor. The motor has no brushes or commutator, and its rotor is a cage of metal bars joined at each end by a ring.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the stator as the source of a rotating magnetic field, and the rotor cage as the part where currents are induced, which turns the rotor
2 marks: Outlines the role of the stator or the rotor cage, with some accurate detail
1 mark: Identifies the stator or the rotor as a part of the motor
markerNotes: Give the stator its job: its coils, fed by AC, produce the rotating magnetic field.
For the rotor, say that currents are induced in the bars, rather than that the rotor is simply pushed.
Mention what is absent, such as brushes, when it helps explain why the motor is robust.
commonStudentErrors: Says the rotor is connected to the supply through brushes, which this motor does not have.
Describes the stator as the part that spins, when it is the fixed part.
Says the rotor is powered directly by the supply, when its current is induced.

sampleAnswers.answer: The stator is fed by the AC supply, and its coils produce a rotating magnetic field. The rotor cage is made of conducting bars joined by end rings. The rotating field induces currents in these bars, and the forces on those currents turn the rotor and the saw blade. The AC induction motor has no brushes or commutator, so no electrical contact is needed to the rotor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining the rotating field from the stator and the induced currents that turn the rotor. The middle answer describes the parts in general terms, without the field or the induced currents.

sampleAnswers.answer: The stator is the fixed part with coils, and the rotor is the part that spins inside it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining the stator and rotor in general terms. It does not explain the rotating magnetic field or the induced currents.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor has a stator and a rotor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying the parts. It gives no role for either one.

prompts.question: DISCUSS how the components of the AC induction motor are designed to support its function and operation in this application, and the points the manager should weigh up.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A factory manager is choosing between an AC induction motor and a DC motor with brushes and a commutator to drive a continuous conveyor belt. The manager is concerned about maintenance and the cost of replacing worn parts.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the components of the AC induction motor support its function and operation, and weighs up the advantages against the limitations for the conveyor belt
5 marks: Discusses the components and operation of the AC induction motor with relevant detail, and identifies both an advantage and a limitation
4 marks: Describes the design of the components and their function with some relevant detail, without weighing up the trade-offs
3 marks: Describes one feature of the motor and its role in its operation, with limited reference to the application
2 marks: Identifies a feature of the AC induction motor, with minimal explanation
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about electric motors
markerNotes: Tie each design feature, such as the rotor cage or the lack of brushes, to a specific function or operation.
Weigh up both sides: the advantages for this belt and the limitations, such as speed control and starting current.
Refer back to the manager's concerns about maintenance, so the discussion stays on the application.
commonStudentErrors: Lists features of the motor without saying how any of them supports its function.
Argues only for the AC induction motor and never gives a limitation, so the discussion is one-sided.
Says the AC induction motor needs brushes to transfer current to the rotor.

sampleAnswers.answer: The AC induction motor suits a conveyor belt because its components are designed for reliable, continuous operation. The stator coils are fed by the AC supply and produce a rotating magnetic field, and the rotor is a cage of conducting bars. The rotating field induces currents in these bars, and the forces on those currents turn the rotor and the belt. Because the motor has no brushes or commutator, there are fewer parts to wear and spark, so it needs less maintenance than a DC motor. Laminated iron cores reduce eddy currents and concentrate the magnetic flux, which supports the motor's function. The manager should weigh these strengths against the limitations: speed control is less simple than in a DC motor and usually needs an electronic drive, and the starting current is high.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by showing how the components support the motor's function and operation, and weighing the advantages against the limitations for the belt. The middle answer describes the design but does not weigh up the trade-offs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The AC induction motor has a stator with coils that produce a rotating magnetic field, and a rotor that turns in response. It has no brushes, so there is less wear than in a DC motor, which suits a conveyor belt.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by describing the design of the components and their function with some relevant detail. It does not weigh up the trade-offs, so it cannot reach the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: An AC induction motor is reliable, so the manager may want to buy one.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying one feature of the motor with minimal explanation. It does not refer to any component.

dotPoints.description: Explain how electromagnetic induction causes a torque on the armature of a brushless DC motor

prompts.question: DESCRIBE how the rotating permanent magnets induce an emf in the armature windings, and what this induced emf opposes.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small drone uses a brushless DC motor to turn its propeller. The motor has permanent magnets on its rotor and a set of armature windings, and an electronic controller switches current through the windings in sequence.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the changing magnetic flux through the armature windings as the magnets turn, and states that the induced emf opposes the supply voltage
2 marks: Describes the changing magnetic flux through the armature windings as the magnets turn, without stating what the induced emf opposes
1 mark: Identifies that the motor's magnets and windings interact to produce a voltage
markerNotes: Name the process as electromagnetic induction, and link it to the changing flux rather than to the magnets alone.
State that the induced emf opposes the supply, which is Lenz's law at work.
Refer to the coils as armature windings, since they are the parts that carry the current.
commonStudentErrors: Says the magnets produce an emf directly, without a changing magnetic flux through the windings.
Says the induced emf adds to the supply voltage, when it opposes it.
Describes the magnets turning without linking this to the windings.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this brushless DC motor, the rotating permanent magnets change the magnetic flux through the armature windings. This is electromagnetic induction: the changing flux induces an emf in the windings. By Lenz's law, the induced emf opposes the change that produces it, so it acts against the supply voltage that drives the current. This induced emf is the back emf of the motor.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by describing the changing flux through the armature windings and stating that the induced emf opposes the supply. The middle answer describes the changing flux but does not say what the emf opposes.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the magnets turn, the magnetic flux through the armature windings changes, which induces a voltage in the windings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the changing flux that induces a voltage. It does not say what the induced emf opposes, so it cannot reach the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The motor uses electromagnetic induction, so its magnets and windings interact.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by identifying an interaction between the magnets and windings. It does not describe the changing flux.

prompts.question: JUSTIFY whether the student's claim is correct, referring to the current in the armature windings and to electromagnetic induction.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that the torque on the armature of a brushless DC motor is produced directly by the induced emf, so a stronger induced emf always gives a larger torque. The student's reasoning ignores the role of the current.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, explaining that torque depends on the current in the armature windings, while the induced emf depends on speed and sets the power
5 marks: Justifies that the claim is incorrect, with a sound explanation of the force on the current in the armature windings
4 marks: Explains that torque depends on the current in the armature, with some reasoning about the induced emf
3 marks: Describes the armature and the induced emf, with limited reasoning about the torque
2 marks: Identifies a relationship between the induced emf and the torque, with minimal reasoning
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about brushless DC motors
markerNotes: State that the claim is incorrect in the opening sentence, then support it with the force on the current.
Link the induced emf to speed and power, not to torque directly.
Name electromagnetic induction as the cause of the back emf, so the link to the motor's operation is clear.
commonStudentErrors: Says torque is the induced emf, so a larger emf always gives a larger torque.
Describes the force on the armature without saying what the current depends on.
Says the back emf adds to the supply, when it opposes it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is incorrect. In this brushless DC motor, the torque on the armature comes from the force on the current in the armature windings when they sit in the magnetic field of the rotor magnets, so it depends on the current rather than directly on the induced emf. The rotating magnets change the flux through the windings, and by electromagnetic induction this produces a back emf that opposes the supply. This back emf grows with the speed of the rotor and limits the current the controller can drive through the windings. The power converted to mechanical energy is the back emf times the current, so for a given current the torque is unchanged even when the induced emf is larger at higher speed. The student has confused a larger induced emf with a larger torque: the torque is set by the current, and the induced emf sets how much power that current can deliver.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row by justifying that the claim is incorrect, with torque tied to the current and the induced emf tied to speed and power. The middle answer gets the force-on-current idea but does not link the induced emf to power.

sampleAnswers.answer: The torque comes from the force on the current in the armature windings, so it depends on the current. A larger induced emf does not automatically give a bigger torque.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by explaining that torque depends on the current, with some reasoning about the induced emf. It does not describe electromagnetic induction or the back emf, and it does not link power and speed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Torque and induced emf are both produced in the armature when the motor runs, so they are linked.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by identifying a link between the induced emf and the torque, with minimal reasoning. It does not explain how the link works.

prompts.question: Explain these observations.
markerNotes: Link each balance reading to a stage of the motion: the rise while the magnet speeds up, and the constant maximum at steady speed.
Name the force on the pipe as the reaction to the upward force on the magnet.
Explain the currents: the changing flux induces eddy currents in the copper, which oppose the fall.
commonStudentErrors: Says the reading rises because the magnet gets heavier as it falls.
Describes the eddy currents without saying how their force reaches the balance.
Says the force on the pipe is upward, so the reading falls.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Relates the measurements on the balance to the motion of the magnet and its interactions with the pipe
3 marks: Relates a measurement on the balance to the motion of the magnet and aspects of its interactions with the pipe
2 marks: Describes some aspects of the motion of the magnet and relates this to a measurement on the balance; OR; Describes the motion of the magnet and/or interactions with the pipe

sampleAnswers.answer:
The reading on the scale has two phases.
1. The magnet accelerates to a maximum speed. This results in an increasing change in magnetic flux causing the creation of an increasing electromagnetic force that opposes the constant gravitational force acting on the magnet. The force on the magnet due to this interaction produces an equal and opposite force on the pipe, which results in an increase in the downward force on the scale.
2. The magnet reaches a constant speed when the upward electromagnetic force is equal and opposite to the weight force of the magnet. The force of the magnet on the pipe will be equal to the weight of the magnet. The reading on the scale will then be the weight of the pipe and magnet, shown in grams.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row by linking the balance readings to the induced current in the pipe, the opposing force on the magnet, its reaction on the pipe, and the constant reading once the forces balance. The middle answer describes the falling magnet and its interaction with the pipe, but does not link these to the balance.

sampleAnswers.answer: As the magnet falls, the changing magnetic field induces currents in the copper pipe. These currents push back on the magnet, so it accelerates more slowly than it would in free fall. At first the magnet speeds up, then it reaches a steady speed while still inside the pipe.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by describing the magnet’s motion and its interaction with the pipe: “currents push back on the magnet”. It does not link either to the balance reading. Relating the extra downward force on the pipe to the rise in the reading would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Copper is a good conductor of current.

sampleAnswers.answer: The desk fan's motor makes an energy transformation from electrical energy to the kinetic energy of the rotating blades, and some electrical energy is also lost as heat in the coils and bearings. prompts.question: DISTINGUISH between the energy transformations in a motor and in a generator, to test the student's claim.
