1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the graphs
markerNotes: Analyse both features: a shared gradient, which is h, and different intercepts, which reflect the work functions.
Link the intercepts to the threshold frequency and to kinetic energy at a given frequency.
Draw a conclusion about the photon model, not only a description of the graphs.
commonStudentErrors: Says the lines have different gradients because the metals are different.
Reads the frequency intercept as the work function, rather than as the threshold frequency.
Describes the graphs without saying what the shared gradient shows.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two lines are parallel, with the same gradient, because the gradient is the Planck constant, h, which is the same for every metal. The graphs differ only in their intercepts. The metal with the higher work function has a vertical intercept further below zero, equal to minus the work function, so for any given frequency its maximum kinetic energy is lower. Its line also crosses the frequency axis at a higher threshold frequency, because the threshold frequency equals the work function divided by h. The metal with the lower work function therefore emits photoelectrons at lower frequencies, and gives them more kinetic energy at the same frequency. Both graphs follow the same relationship, Kmax = hf − ϕ, with the metal changing only the work function. Photoelectric experiments on different metals therefore support the photon model: the energy of each photon, hf, is the same for every metal, while the energy needed to escape differs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: explains the shared gradient and the different intercepts, links them to the work function and threshold frequency, and draws a supported conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two lines are parallel because they share the gradient h. They differ in their intercepts, so the metal with the higher work function has a higher threshold frequency and lower kinetic energy at the same frequency.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains the shared gradient and the difference in intercepts, but does not link the result to the photon model in the photoelectric experiments.

sampleAnswers.answer: The two graphs start at different points because the metals have different work functions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies a difference between the graphs and its cause, without analysing the gradient or what the graphs show.

dotPoints.description: Conduct a secondary-source investigation to explain how the photelectric effect is used in photovoltaics (solar cells) and one other real-world application

prompts.question: Using secondary sources, explain how the photoelectric effect is used in photovoltaic solar cells to produce an electric current.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has found secondary sources about rooftop solar panels and must explain the physics in a short written response.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that photons release electrons in a semiconductor of a solar cell, producing a current, and that the energy of each photon decides whether a release occurs
2 marks: Describes the release of electrons by photons in a solar cell, with some reference to the current produced
1 mark: Identifies that solar cells use sunlight to produce electricity
markerNotes: Name the process: photons absorbed in a semiconductor release electrons, which are driven round a circuit as a current.
Say that the energy of each photon decides whether a release occurs, while the number of photons affects how much current flows.
Show what the secondary source supports, rather than only naming the application.
commonStudentErrors: Says the solar cell converts heat from the sun into electricity, rather than using photons.
States that brighter sunlight releases electrons because each photon has more energy.
Describes the photoelectric effect without linking it to photovoltaics or a current.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a solar cell, photons from sunlight strike a semiconductor, and a photon with enough energy transfers its energy to an electron and releases it. This photoelectric effect is the basis of photovoltaics: the freed electrons are driven through an external circuit, producing an electric current. A secondary source shows that the number of electrons released depends on the number of photons absorbed, while the energy of photons decides whether a release happens at all.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains that photons release electrons in a semiconductor, that the freed electrons produce a current, and that photon energy decides whether a release occurs.

sampleAnswers.answer: Photons strike a solar cell and release electrons, which produce a current.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the release of electrons and a current, but does not explain that photon energy decides the release or name photovoltaics.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solar cells use sunlight to produce electricity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the use of sunlight in solar cells without the photoelectric process.

prompts.question: Discuss how the photoelectric effect is applied in photovoltaics and in one other real-world application, and how each application depends on the energy of individual photons.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student has found two secondary sources, one about rooftop solar panels and one about a photomultiplier tube in a medical scanner, and must write a short discussion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the photoelectric effect is applied in both applications, linking each to the energy of individual photons and comparing their outputs
5 marks: Discusses the photoelectric process in photovoltaics and in one other application, with a clear link to the energy of photons
4 marks: Describes both applications and the release of electrons by photons, with some reference to photon energy
3 marks: Describes one application of the photoelectric effect, with limited reference to photons
2 marks: Identifies that electrons released by light are used in photovoltaics or another application
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the photoelectric effect or its uses
markerNotes: Discuss both applications, not only one: the photoelectric release is the common principle, and each application uses it differently.
Link each application to the energy of individual photons, which decides whether a release occurs.
Compare the outputs: a continuous current in a solar cell, and a sensitive pulse in a photomultiplier tube.
commonStudentErrors: Describes only solar cells and never discusses the second application.
Says that a brighter light makes each photon more energetic in both applications.
Treats the photomultiplier tube as producing electricity from heat, rather than from released electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: In photovoltaics, the photoelectric effect takes place in the semiconductor of a solar cell. A photon absorbed by the semiconductor can release an electron only if its energy is high enough to overcome the energy barrier of the material, so the current depends on the energy of photons, not only on the brightness of the sunlight. The freed electrons are separated by an internal electric field and driven through an external circuit, which produces the current. A photomultiplier tube uses the photoelectric effect differently. Light from a scintillation crystal strikes a photocathode, and each photon that is absorbed can release an electron. The released electrons are multiplied through a chain of dynodes, so that a single photon produces a measurable pulse of current. This makes the photomultiplier tube sensitive to very low light levels. In both applications, the energy of photons decides whether a release occurs, while the number of photons determines how much current or signal is produced. The two uses therefore rest on the same principle, with the photoelectric effect applied to produce either a continuous current or a sensitive pulse.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: discusses both applications, links each to the energy of individual photons, and compares the continuous current with the sensitive pulse.

sampleAnswers.answer: In a solar cell, photons with enough energy release electrons in a semiconductor, producing a current. A photomultiplier tube also uses the photoelectric effect, releasing electrons from a photocathode that are multiplied to give a measurable signal.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes both applications and the photoelectric release, but does not discuss how each depends on the energy of individual photons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Solar cells and photomultiplier tubes both use electrons released by light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies electrons released by light in both applications, without describing how the effect is used.

dotPoints.description: Explain how observations of the photoelectric effect and data can validate predictions about the quantum nature of light

prompts.question: Explain how the observed threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect supports the predictions of the photon model of light, and how these data validate the quantum nature of light.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student tests a clean metal surface with light of different frequencies and records the frequency at which electrons first leave the surface.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the threshold frequency matches the photon prediction that each photon must supply the work function, so the data validate the quantum nature of light
2 marks: Relates the threshold frequency to the photon model, with some reference to the predictions being tested
1 mark: Identifies that electrons are emitted only above a threshold frequency
markerNotes: Name the prediction being tested: each photon gives its energy to one electron, so emission needs photon energy at the work function.
Explain why brightness does not matter: the threshold is set by frequency, and extra intensity only adds photons.
Say what the data show, and why a continuous wave model would not predict a threshold.
commonStudentErrors: Says the threshold frequency proves that light is a wave, because the electrons respond to light.
Describes the threshold as a brightness level, rather than a frequency.
States that the data prove the quantum nature of light beyond all doubt.

sampleAnswers.answer: The photoelectric effect supports the quantum nature of light. The photon model predicts that photons give their energy to single electrons, so an electron is emitted only if the energy of each photon reaches the work function. The observed threshold frequency, below which no electrons appear however bright the light, matches this prediction. The data therefore validate the predictions of the photon model, which a continuous wave model does not make.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: links the observed threshold to the photon prediction about the work function, and states that the data validate the quantum nature of light.

sampleAnswers.answer: The photon model predicts that each photon gives its energy to one electron. The observed threshold frequency matches this, so the photon model is supported.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: relates the threshold frequency to the photon model, but does not explain why brightness is irrelevant or why a wave model would differ.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons are emitted from the metal only above a threshold frequency.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the threshold observation without linking it to a prediction.

prompts.question: Assess how measurements of maximum kinetic energy against frequency for several metals validate the predictions of the photon model and support the quantum nature of light, using the gradient of the graphs.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class plots the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency for three different metals and obtains three straight, parallel lines.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses how the common gradient and the different intercepts validate the predictions, explains why a wave model cannot give this result, and reaches a justified judgement on the strength of the evidence
5 marks: Assesses the common gradient across the metals and explains why it is a meaningful test of the photon model
4 marks: Explains that the parallel lines match the photon model prediction for the gradient and the intercepts, with some reference to the quantum nature of light
3 marks: Describes the straight lines and their shared gradient, with limited reference to the predictions
2 marks: Identifies that the graphs are straight lines, with a link to the photoelectric effect
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the photoelectric effect
markerNotes: Assess the strength of the evidence: a common gradient across several metals is a meaningful test, not one measurement.
Name the prediction: the gradient is the Planck constant, the same for every metal, while the intercepts depend on the work function.
Explain why a wave model fails: it links the energy to intensity, not to frequency, so it predicts no common gradient.
commonStudentErrors: Says three straight lines prove the theory, without assessing how strong the evidence is.
Reads the common gradient as showing that all metals have the same work function.
Describes the lines without saying which prediction they test.

sampleAnswers.answer: The photoelectric effect data validate the predictions of the photon model, because the model predicts a precise linear relation between maximum kinetic energy and frequency. Each graph is a straight line, so the energy rises in proportion to frequency above the threshold, as the quantum nature of light requires. The stronger test is the gradient. The model predicts that the gradient is the Planck constant, h, the same for every metal, while the intercepts differ with the work function. Three parallel lines with a common gradient confirm this. A wave model would predict that the energy depends on intensity rather than frequency, so it gives no reason for a common gradient. Had the gradients differed between metals, the photon model would have been falsified, so the agreement is a meaningful test. A single set of observations cannot prove the theory, but a common gradient across several metals supports the quantum nature of light and gives the data real weight.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: assesses the common gradient as a meaningful test, explains why a wave model fails it, and reaches a justified judgement on the strength of the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The three parallel lines match the photon model. The gradient is the same for each metal, as predicted, while the intercepts differ with the work function. This supports the quantum nature of light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains the parallel lines against the prediction for the gradient and intercepts, but does not assess how strong the evidence is.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graphs are straight lines, and they show a link between frequency and energy in the photoelectric effect.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies straight-line graphs and a link to the photoelectric effect, without a prediction being tested.

dotPoints.description: Compare inertial and non-inertial frames of reference

prompts.question: Compare an inertial frame of reference with a non-inertial frame of reference, using a car that brakes suddenly as an example.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A passenger in a car that brakes suddenly lurches forward, while a passenger in a car travelling at a steady speed along a straight road feels no push.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Compares constant velocity in an inertial frame with acceleration or rotation in a non-inertial frame, and links the apparent push in the braking car to a fictitious force
2 marks: Compares the motion of objects in an inertial frame and a non-inertial frame, with some reference to the braking car
1 mark: Identifies that a non-inertial frame of reference is one that accelerates
markerNotes: Compare the two frames on the same features: whether the frame accelerates, and whether objects appear to accelerate with no net force.
Use the car example to show that the apparent push is a fictitious force in the non-inertial frame, not a real force.
Name the frames clearly: an inertial frame at constant velocity, and a non-inertial frame that accelerates or rotates.
commonStudentErrors: Says the passenger is pushed by a real force from the seat when the car brakes.
States that an inertial frame must be at rest.
Says a moving car is always a non-inertial frame of reference.

sampleAnswers.answer: An inertial frame of reference moves at constant velocity, so no net force acts and Newton's first law holds. A non-inertial frame of reference accelerates or rotates, so objects in it appear to accelerate without a net force. In the car example, the passenger in the steadily moving car feels no push, while the passenger in the braking car appears to be thrown forward, which is explained only by a fictitious force in that non-inertial frame of reference.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: compares constant velocity with acceleration or rotation, and links the apparent push in the braking car to a fictitious force.

sampleAnswers.answer: An inertial frame moves at constant velocity, but a non-inertial frame accelerates. Objects in the braking car appear to be pushed forward.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: compares the motion in each frame and uses the braking car, but does not explain that the push is a fictitious force.

sampleAnswers.answer: A non-inertial frame of reference is one that accelerates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the accelerating frame, without a comparison with the inertial frame.

prompts.question: A student claims that an observer in any moving vehicle is in a non-inertial frame of reference, so the laws of physics are not the same for that observer as for a stationary one. Analyse the difference between inertial and non-inertial frames of reference to test this claim.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student rides in a train that moves at a steady speed along straight tracks and drops a ball from hand height.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the difference between constant velocity and acceleration in each frame, applies it to the steady train, and tests the claim with a justified judgement
5 marks: Analyses why an accelerating or rotating frame needs a fictitious force, and applies the distinction to the steady train
4 marks: Explains that an inertial frame has constant velocity and a non-inertial frame accelerates, with some application to the claim
3 marks: Describes the motion of objects in inertial and non-inertial frames, with limited reference to the claim
2 marks: Identifies that a steady train is an inertial frame, with a verdict on the claim
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about frames of reference
markerNotes: Test the claim against the train: a vehicle at steady speed in a straight line is inertial, so the claim is false for that journey.
Explain the non-inertial case: an accelerating or rotating frame makes objects seem to accelerate, which needs a fictitious force.
Say when the claim would be true: only if the train braked, turned or sped up.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the claim because any observer in motion feels forces that are not real.
Confuses motion at constant velocity with acceleration.
States that a ball dropped in a train falls at an angle, which would show a non-inertial frame.

sampleAnswers.answer: The claim is not correct. A frame of reference is inertial when it moves at constant velocity, with no acceleration, so the train moving at a steady speed along straight tracks is an inertial frame. In that frame a dropped ball falls straight down with no net force acting sideways, and the same laws of physics apply as for a stationary observer on the platform. A non-inertial frame of reference, by contrast, accelerates or rotates. In such a frame, objects seem to accelerate without any net force, and this apparent effect is explained by a fictitious force. Examples include the forward lurch of a braking car and the outward push felt on a rotating carousel. The student has confused motion at constant velocity with acceleration. A vehicle moving at steady speed in a straight line gives an inertial frame, and only a vehicle that speeds up, slows down or turns creates a non-inertial frame. The claim is therefore false for a steady, straight-line journey, although it would be true for a train that brakes or turns.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: separates constant velocity from acceleration in each frame, applies this to the steady train, and tests the claim with a justified judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: An inertial frame moves at constant velocity, with no net force on objects. A non-inertial frame accelerates or rotates, and objects in it appear to accelerate, which needs a fictitious force. So the steady train is inertial, and the claim is false.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains the two frames and applies them to the train, but does not analyse why the fictitious force is needed or when the claim would be true.

sampleAnswers.answer: A train at steady speed is an inertial frame, because it is not accelerating. So the claim is wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the steady train as inertial and gives a verdict, without explaining the difference between the frames.

dotPoints.description: Outline Einstein’s first and second postulates of special relativity

prompts.question: Outline the two postulates of special relativity, stating what each says about the laws of physics and the speed of light in inertial frames.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is asked to explain how Einstein's postulates describe measurements made by a pilot in a fast-moving spacecraft and by an observer on the ground.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the first postulate, that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and the second, that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers
2 marks: Outlines one postulate accurately, or both postulates with limited detail
1 mark: Identifies that the speed of light is constant
markerNotes: Outline both postulates, not only one: the laws of physics are the same in inertial frames, and the speed of light is constant.
State that the speed of light is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.
Keep the frames inertial: the postulates describe frames at constant velocity.
commonStudentErrors: Says the first postulate means that all frames move at the same speed.
States that the second postulate says light speed changes with the motion of the source.
Describes the postulates without naming the speed of light.

sampleAnswers.answer: The first postulate states that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference, so no inertial frame is special. The second postulate states that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer. Together, these postulates form the basis of special relativity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: outlines both postulates, the laws of physics in inertial frames and the constant speed of light in a vacuum.

sampleAnswers.answer: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. The speed of light is the same for all observers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: outlines both postulates briefly, without the vacuum or the note about inertial frames.

sampleAnswers.answer: Light always travels at the same speed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the constant speed of light, without the first postulate or the frames.

prompts.question: Discuss why Einstein's second postulate, that the speed of light is the same for all observers, was a departure from everyday ideas about adding velocities, and how it relates to the first postulate.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student argues that if a torch is carried on a moving train and switched on while the train moves forward, its light should travel faster than c relative to the track.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses why the constant speed of light departs from everyday velocity addition, and links the result to the first postulate and the principle of relativity
5 marks: Discusses the conflict with everyday velocity addition and explains why the second postulate follows from the first
4 marks: Explains that the speed of light is the same for all observers, so the torch's light is not faster than c, with some reference to the postulates
3 marks: Describes everyday velocity addition and contrasts it with the constant speed of light, with limited reference to the postulates
2 marks: Identifies that light has the same speed for all observers, unlike everyday velocities
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about velocities or light
markerNotes: Contrast everyday velocity addition with light: a thrown ball adds to the train's speed, but the light from the torch does not.
Link the second postulate to the first: if the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, every observer must measure the same speed for light.
Reject the student's claim clearly, and say that the second postulate is a result of the first.
commonStudentErrors: Says the light from the torch would move faster than c, because velocities always add.
Treats the second postulate as an arbitrary assumption, rather than a consequence of the first.
States that the speed of light changes with the speed of the observer.

sampleAnswers.answer: Everyday experience suggests that velocities add: a ball thrown forward from a moving train should travel faster than the train alone. Einstein's postulates, and in particular the second postulate, depart from this idea for light. The speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer, so light emitted forward from a moving train travels at c relative to the track, not at c plus the speed of the train. The student's argument, that the light from the torch would exceed c, therefore fails. The first postulate explains why the second must hold: if the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, including the laws of electromagnetism that predict a fixed speed for light, then every inertial observer must measure the same speed. The second postulate is therefore a consequence of the principle of relativity, not an arbitrary assumption, and it forces changes in how space and time are measured by observers in relative motion, as special relativity describes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: contrasts velocity addition with the constant speed of light, links the second postulate to the first, and rejects the student's claim with reasons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Everyday velocities add, but the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers. So a torch on a moving train does not emit light faster than c. This is the second postulate of special relativity, which conflicts with everyday ideas about velocities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains the constant speed of light and applies it to the torch, but does not explain why the second postulate follows from the first.

sampleAnswers.answer: Light has the same speed for all observers, unlike the everyday rule for adding velocities.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the constant speed of light and the contrast with everyday velocities, without an application to the torch.

dotPoints.description: Apply Einstein’s first and second postulates of special relativity to a simultaneity thought experiment involving 2 events occurring at opposite ends of a vehicle moving at relativistic speed when viewed from different frames of reference

prompts.question: Explain, using Einstein's postulates, why an observer at the centre of a moving vehicle concludes that two flashes of light at the ends of the vehicle are simultaneous.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A vehicle travels at a relativistic speed along a straight track. Two flashes of light occur at its front and rear ends at the same instant as judged from inside the vehicle.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that light travels at the speed of light in the vehicle frame, and that the observer at the centre is equidistant from both ends, so simultaneity holds in the frame of reference of the vehicle
2 marks: Relates the equal distances from the centre to simultaneous arrival of light, with some reference to the postulates
1 mark: Identifies that the light from both flashes reaches the centre of the vehicle at the same time
markerNotes: Use the second postulate: light travels at the same speed in the vehicle frame, so the timing of its arrival is a fair test.
Explain why the centre observer is special: she is equidistant from both ends, so simultaneous arrival means simultaneous flashes in her frame.
Say that simultaneity is judged within a frame of reference, not as an absolute fact.
commonStudentErrors: Says the flashes are simultaneous for everyone, because light always arrives at the same time.
Ignores the centre position, so the reasoning does not depend on equal distances.
States that the vehicle speed changes the time the light takes to reach the centre.

sampleAnswers.answer: Einstein's postulates imply that light travels at the speed of light, c, in every inertial frame of reference. In the vehicle frame, the observer at the centre is equidistant from both ends, so light from the two flashes reaches her together. She concludes that the flashes are simultaneous in her frame, even at relativistic speed. Simultaneity therefore depends on the frame of reference.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: uses the constant speed of light and equal distances to show simultaneity in the vehicle frame, and notes that simultaneity depends on the frame of reference.

sampleAnswers.answer: The observer is at the centre of the vehicle, so the light from both ends reaches her together. Light travels at the same speed in her frame, so the flashes are simultaneous for her.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: relates the equal distances to simultaneous arrival and uses the constant speed of light, but does not state that simultaneity depends on the frame of reference.

sampleAnswers.answer: The light from both flashes reaches the centre of the vehicle at the same time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies simultaneous arrival at the centre, without the reasoning from the postulates.

prompts.question: Apply Einstein's postulates to the same two flashes, as viewed by a stationary observer on the ground, to show that the flashes are not simultaneous in that frame.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The same two flashes that were simultaneous for the observer at the centre of the vehicle are now viewed by a stationary observer on the ground while the vehicle moves at relativistic speed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Applies both postulates to the ground frame, explains why light speed is unchanged while the time of each event changes, and concludes that the flashes are not simultaneous there
5 marks: Applies the postulates to the ground frame and explains why the vehicle's motion changes the order of the two events, with a clear conclusion
4 marks: Explains that the vehicle's motion at relativistic speed makes the events not simultaneous in the ground frame, with some reference to the postulates
3 marks: Describes that the ground observer judges the flashes at different times, with limited reference to the postulates
2 marks: Identifies that the vehicle's motion changes the timing of the two flashes for the ground observer
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about simultaneity or frames of reference
markerNotes: Apply the second postulate to the ground frame: light from each flash still travels at c, so the difference lies in the timing of the events.
Explain the order: the ground observer finds the rear flash first, because the vehicle moves and events are judged at different times along it.
Conclude clearly that simultaneity depends on the frame of reference, so both observers are correct in their own frames.
commonStudentErrors: Says that the flashes must be simultaneous in every frame, because they were simultaneous for the vehicle observer.
Claims that the light from the flashes travels faster in the ground frame.
Says the ground observer is wrong, rather than judging the flashes in another frame.

sampleAnswers.answer: Einstein's postulates imply that the two flashes are simultaneous in the frame of the vehicle, where the centre observer sees both light signals arrive together. The ground observer does not share that conclusion. By the first postulate, the laws of physics, including those describing light, are the same in both inertial frames, so neither frame is privileged. By the second postulate, the speed of light is c for the ground observer as well, so the light from each flash still travels at c. What changes is the time at which each event is judged to occur. Since the vehicle moves forward at relativistic speed, the ground frame assigns different times to events at different positions along the vehicle, so the flash at the rear is judged to happen first. The ground observer therefore concludes that the two flashes are not simultaneous. Both observers are correct within their own frame of reference, and the difference shows that simultaneity depends on the frame, a consequence of the constant speed of light rather than a measurement error.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: applies both postulates to the ground frame, explains why the order of the flashes changes, and concludes that they are not simultaneous there.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ground observer sees the flashes differently from the vehicle observer. Light still travels at c for both, but the vehicle moves at relativistic speed, so the events are judged at different times in the ground frame and the rear flash comes first.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains the change in timing with the postulates and the relativistic speed, but does not explain how the ground frame assigns different times along the vehicle.

sampleAnswers.answer: The vehicle moves, so the two flashes are not simultaneous for the ground observer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies that the motion changes the timing of the flashes, without applying the postulates.

dotPoints.description: Apply Einstein’s first and second postulates of special relativity to a time dilation thought experiment involving light pulses reflecting inside a vehicle moving at relativistic speed when viewed from different frames of reference

prompts.question: Explain why an observer on the ground measures a longer time between light reflections in a vehicle than the observer inside the vehicle does.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A light pulse bounces between two mirrors fixed to the floor and ceiling of a vehicle moving at relativistic speed along a straight road.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the light pulse travels a longer diagonal path in the ground frame at the same speed of light, so the time interval is longer, which is time dilation
2 marks: Relates the longer path in the ground frame to a longer time interval, with some reference to the speed of light
1 mark: Identifies that the ground observer measures a longer time between reflections
markerNotes: Describe the two paths: straight up and down in the vehicle, and a longer diagonal path for the ground observer.
Use the second postulate: the pulse travels at the same speed in both frames, so the longer path gives a longer time.
Name the result as time dilation: the moving clock runs slow as seen from the ground.
commonStudentErrors: Says the ground observer measures a shorter time, because the vehicle moves toward the mirrors.
Claims that the light pulse travels faster in the ground frame, so it takes less time.
Gives the path length as the same in both frames.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both observers see the light pulse travel at the speed of light, c, because the postulates require the same speed in every inertial frame of reference. Inside the vehicle, the pulse goes straight up and down between the mirrors. The ground observer sees a longer diagonal path, because the vehicle moves at relativistic speed while the light moves. Since the speed of light is the same, the longer path means a longer time interval, which is time dilation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains the longer diagonal path at the same speed of light, and links it to a longer interval as time dilation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pulse travels straight up and down in the vehicle, but along a longer diagonal path on the ground. Light moves at c for both, so the ground observer measures more time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: relates the longer path to the longer time with the speed of light, but does not name the result as time dilation or the postulates.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ground observer measures a longer time between reflections than the observer in the vehicle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the longer time as measured on the ground, without the reason.

prompts.question: Analyse how the first and second postulates together require both observers to agree on the speed of light but disagree on the time between reflections in the light-pulse thought experiment.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student argues that since both observers see the light pulse move at the speed of light, both must measure the same time between reflections inside the vehicle.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the postulates require the same speed of light and a different time interval, applies this to the vehicle, and tests the student's argument with a justified judgement
5 marks: Analyses why the longer diagonal path in the ground frame gives a longer time interval, and explains time dilation in the vehicle
4 marks: Explains that both observers agree on the speed of light, but the ground observer measures a longer time, with some reference to the student's argument
3 marks: Describes the light-pulse paths in the two frames, with limited reference to the postulates
2 marks: Identifies that the ground observer measures a longer time between reflections
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the light pulse or the postulates
markerNotes: Explain what the postulates fix: the speed of light is the same for both observers, which is the common ground of the argument.
Explain what they leave open: the time interval depends on the path, so the frames can measure different times.
Reach a judgement on the student's argument, and say why the disagreement is not an error.
commonStudentErrors: Concludes that equal speeds of light mean equal time intervals for both observers.
Says that time dilation is caused by the light pulse slowing down.
Claims that the disagreement shows one observer has made a measurement error.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student is partly right and partly wrong. Both observers agree that the light pulse travels at the speed of light, c, because the postulates hold in every inertial frame of reference. However, the first postulate says that the laws of physics, including the way a light clock works, are the same in both frames, so the two observers describe the same process in different ways. Inside the vehicle, the pulse goes straight up between the mirrors and back, so the time between reflections is set by the height between the mirrors and c. For the ground observer, the vehicle moves at relativistic speed while the pulse moves, so the pulse follows a longer diagonal path. Because the speed is the same in both frames, the longer path takes longer, and the ground observer measures a longer time between reflections. This is time dilation: the moving clock runs slow as seen from the ground. Both observers are correct in their own frame of reference, and the disagreement arises because time intervals depend on the frame, not because either measurement is in error.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: separates the agreed speed of light from the disagreed time interval, applies this to the vehicle, and rejects the student's argument with reasons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Both observers agree the light pulse moves at c, but the ground observer sees a longer diagonal path. Since the speed is the same, the longer path gives a longer time between reflections, which is time dilation. So the student's conclusion is wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains that the speed is shared and the time differs, and rejects the student's conclusion, but does not analyse the postulates as separate requirements.

sampleAnswers.answer: The light pulse moves at c for both observers, but the ground observer records a longer time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the shared speed and the longer time on the ground, without a judgement on the student's argument.

dotPoints.description: Account for the relativistic effects of time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum from an external frame of reference

prompts.question: Analyse the consequences of the theory of special relativity in relation to length, time and motion. Support your answer with reference to experimental evidence.
markerNotes: Analyse each consequence (time, length and motion) from the two postulates, not only define it.
Support at least one consequence with experimental evidence, such as the muon flux, and say what the evidence shows.
Name the frame of reference in each effect: who measures what.
commonStudentErrors: Lists time dilation and length contraction as definitions without linking them to the postulates.
Refers to the muon evidence without saying in which frame the effect is observed.
Says an object's mass increases with speed, rather than its relativistic momentum.
prompts.markingCriteria:
8 marks: Provides a comprehensive analysis of the consequences of special relativity on time, length and motion; Refers to applicable experimental evidence
6-7 marks: Provides a thorough analysis of the consequences of special relativity on time, length and motion; Refers to applicable experimental evidence
4-5 marks: Provides analysis of the consequences of special relativity on time and/or length and/or motion; Refers to some relevant experimental evidence
2-3 marks: Makes some reference to special relativity and/or related experimental evidence
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
The two postulates of special relativity are: the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant, and all inertial frames of reference are equivalent.
The consequences of these postulates are time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum dilation. Time dilation means that the measured time between events increases as the speed of an observer increases. Length contraction means that the length of an object decreases as the speed of an observer increases, and relativistic momentum dilation means that objects (with mass) cannot travel at c as it takes increasing amounts of energy to accelerate objects as they approach the speed of light.
Length contraction and time dilation can both be seen in observations of muons at Earth’s surface. The short half-life of muons suggests that there should be very few of them that arrive at Earth’s surface from their point of origin high in Earth’s atmosphere, but the muon flux is greater than suggested by half-life and distance travelled alone. However, when the distance travelled is considered from the muon’s frame of reference, it is length-contracted according to l = l₀√(1 − v²/c²), giving an effective shorter distance for them to travel. From the perspective of an observer on Earth’s surface, the time taken for them to decay is dilated, giving an effective greater amount of time for them to travel before decaying.
The effects of relativistic momentum can be seen in particle accelerators in terms of the increasing amounts of energy to required to accelerate the particles as they approach the speed of light – it is though the objects are much more massive than they are.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 8-mark row: the postulates are used to analyse time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum for different observers, with muon and particle evidence. The middle answer analyses time and length with one piece of evidence but does not analyse motion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, and the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. One consequence is time dilation. A moving clock runs slow when observed from a frame in which it moves, so the time between events is longer for that observer. Another is length contraction, in which a moving object is shorter along its direction of motion. Muons created high in the atmosphere reach the ground in greater numbers than their short half-life predicts, which is evidence for time dilation as seen from Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row by analysing time dilation and length contraction from the postulates and supporting them with the muon evidence. It does not analyse the effect on motion or momentum, which the 6-7 row needs, so adding how the energy needed to accelerate an object grows as it nears c would lift it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Special relativity says the speed of light is the same for all observers, and that moving clocks run slow. Experiments with fast particles have confirmed time dilation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-3 mark row by referring to special relativity and to related experimental evidence. It gives no analysis of time, length or motion, and explaining how the time interval changes for an observer would lift it to the 4-5 row.

prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–36. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Solve quantitative problems involving t = t₀ / √(1 − v² / c²), lv = l₀√(1 − v² / c²) and pv = m₀v / √(1 − v² / c²)
Explain why an object with mass cannot travel at the speed of light

prompts.question: Explain why the energy needed to speed up an object with mass increases as its speed approaches the speed of light.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student proposes that a rocket with a large fuel supply could keep accelerating until it reaches the speed of light.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the relativistic energy and momentum of an object with mass grow without limit as its speed approaches the speed of light, so reaching it would need infinite energy
2 marks: Relates the increase in energy or mass to speed, with some reference to the speed of light
1 mark: Identifies that an object with mass cannot reach the speed of light
markerNotes: Name the trend: the energy needed for each further increase in speed grows without limit as the speed approaches c.
Conclude that reaching c would need infinite energy, which no finite fuel supply can provide, so c is a limit for objects with mass.
Mention photons as the exception: they have no rest mass, so they travel at c.
commonStudentErrors: Says an object with mass cannot reach the speed of light because it is too heavy to move that fast.
States that the object's mass becomes zero at the speed of light.
Says a more powerful rocket would reach the speed of light given enough time.

sampleAnswers.answer: As an object with mass speeds up, its relativistic momentum and energy increase, and the energy needed for each further increase in speed grows without limit. Reaching the speed of light would therefore require an infinite amount of energy, which no finite fuel supply can provide. This is why a rocket with more fuel still cannot reach the speed of light. Photons have no rest mass, so they can travel at the speed of light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains the unlimited growth of energy and momentum as the speed approaches c, and the need for infinite energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: As speed increases, the energy needed to accelerate a massive object grows, so the object cannot reach the speed of light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: relates energy to speed and to the speed of light, but does not explain why the energy grows without limit.

sampleAnswers.answer: An object with mass would need infinite energy to reach the speed of light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the impossibility without the trend in energy as speed rises.

prompts.question: A student argues that an object with only a very small mass should be able to reach the speed of light, since photons travel at that speed. Analyse the relationship between mass, energy and speed to test this argument.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student argues that an object with only a very small mass should be able to reach the speed of light, because photons travel at that speed.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the energy and relativistic momentum of an object with rest mass grow without limit near the speed of light, and tests the argument with a justified judgement
5 marks: Analyses why a small mass does not remove the limit, and distinguishes a small mass from zero rest mass
4 marks: Explains that the energy needed to reach the speed of light is infinite for any object with mass, with some reference to photons
3 marks: Describes the link between mass, energy and speed, with limited reference to the speed of light
2 marks: Identifies that photons travel at the speed of light, and that an object with mass cannot
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about photons or mass
markerNotes: Distinguish a small mass from zero mass: photons have zero rest mass, while the student's object has some rest mass.
Explain the limit: the energy needed grows without limit near c, and a smaller mass only lowers the energy at a given speed.
Reach a clear judgement on the argument, and say what the exception of photons shows.
commonStudentErrors: Accepts the argument because photons travel at the speed of light.
Treats a very small mass as if it were zero mass.
States that a smaller mass reduces the energy needed to infinity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The argument does not hold, however small the mass. Photons travel at the speed of light because they have no rest mass, and this is a special case, not a route open to any object with some mass. For an object with mass, the energy needed to increase its speed rises without limit as the speed approaches the speed of light, because the relativistic momentum and energy grow faster as the speed approaches c. A small mass only means that a smaller total energy is needed at a given speed; it does not remove the limit, because the energy required still becomes infinite at c. Therefore no finite energy can accelerate even a very small mass to the speed of light. The student has treated a small mass as if it were zero mass, which is a different case. The relationship between mass, energy and speed shows that c is a limit for every object with mass, while photons, which have zero rest mass, are the exception that always travels at the speed of light in a vacuum.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: separates a small mass from zero rest mass, shows why the energy stays unlimited near c, and gives a justified judgement on the argument.

sampleAnswers.answer: Photons travel at the speed of light because they have zero rest mass, not because they have a small mass. An object with any mass needs more energy as its speed rises, and this energy becomes infinite at c, so it cannot reach the speed of light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-mark row: explains the infinite energy for any object with mass and contrasts photons, but does not analyse why a small mass leaves the limit in place.

sampleAnswers.answer: Photons travel at the speed of light, but an object with a small mass still cannot reach it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies the photon exception and the limit for objects with mass, without analysis of the energy.

dotPoints.description: Analyse the evidence supporting the theory of relativity, including the muon lifetime and atomic clocks moving at different velocities

prompts.question: Explain how the measured muon flux at Earth's surface supports the theory of relativity, including the muon lifetime.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student reads that muons created high in the atmosphere reach the ground in large numbers, and must explain the evidence in a short written response.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the muon flux at the surface, greater than the short muon lifetime allows, is evidence of time dilation in the theory of relativity
2 marks: Describes the muon lifetime and the surface flux, with some reference to time dilation
1 mark: Identifies muons at the surface as evidence for the theory of relativity
markerNotes: Compare the expected and measured numbers: a short muon lifetime predicts few muons at the surface, but many are detected.
Explain the time dilation: from the Earth frame, the high speed of the muon extends its lifetime.
Say what the evidence supports: the theory of relativity, not only a single number.
commonStudentErrors: Says muons reach the ground because they are not affected by the atmosphere.
States that muons live longer because they are heavier.
Describes the muon evidence without linking it to time dilation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Muons created high in the atmosphere have a very short muon lifetime, so few would reach the ground if that were the only factor. Yet a large muon flux is detected at the surface, which is evidence of time dilation: from the Earth frame, the high speed of the muon extends its lifetime. This supports the theory of relativity, because the muon lifetime is longer for the moving muons than the stationary value predicts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains that the muon flux exceeds what the short muon lifetime allows, and links the excess to time dilation in the theory of relativity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Muons have a short lifetime, but many reach the ground. Time dilation extends the muon lifetime for an observer on Earth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the muon lifetime and the surface flux, and links them to time dilation, but does not state the theory of relativity as the support.

sampleAnswers.answer: Muons detected at Earth's surface are evidence for the theory of relativity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies muons at the surface as evidence, without the reasoning.

prompts.question: Analyse the evidence from the muon lifetime and from atomic clocks moving at different velocities, to show how it supports the theory of relativity.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student finds two sources, one describing muon counts at the surface and one describing clocks flown on aircraft, and is asked to link them to the theory of relativity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses both lines of evidence, linking the muon lifetime and the clock differences to time dilation, and judges how far they support the theory of relativity
5 marks: Analyses the muon lifetime and the atomic clocks, with a clear link to time dilation and the velocities involved
4 marks: Explains the muon evidence and the clock evidence separately, with some reference to the theory of relativity
3 marks: Describes one line of evidence, with limited reference to time dilation
2 marks: Identifies that muons and moving atomic clocks give evidence for the theory of relativity
1 mark: Provides some relevant information about the muon lifetime or atomic clocks
markerNotes: Analyse both sets of evidence: the muon flux and the clock differences, each linked to time dilation at a particular velocity.
Explain the frames: the muon's frame and the Earth frame give the same surviving count, through different routes.
Judge the strength: the evidence agrees with the theory in direction and size, but tests specific cases rather than the whole theory.
commonStudentErrors: Treats the muon and clock evidence as separate, with no link to time dilation.
Says the atomic clocks prove the theory of relativity beyond all doubt.
Says moving clocks run faster, rather than slower, than clocks on the ground.

sampleAnswers.answer: Two independent lines of evidence support the theory of relativity. First, the muon lifetime appears longer for muons travelling at high speed. Muons are created high in the atmosphere and decay quickly, yet a large flux reaches the surface. From the Earth frame, time dilation extends the muon lifetime, so more muons survive the journey; from the muon's frame, the atmosphere is length-contracted, which gives the same surviving count. Second, atomic clocks moving at different velocities keep different time. In a well-known experiment, caesium clocks flown around the world were compared with clocks left on the ground, and the moving clocks showed the predicted differences in elapsed time. Gravitational effects were also involved, and the observed differences matched the relativistic predictions once both were included. The two sets of evidence agree in direction and size with the theory, which predicts that moving clocks run slow. Their weakness is that they test specific cases, not all of relativity, so the theory is supported rather than proved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: analyses the muon lifetime and the moving clocks through time dilation, and judges that the evidence supports the theory without proving it.

sampleAnswers.answer: Muons have a short lifetime but many reach the ground, which time dilation explains. Atomic clocks flown on aircraft run at different rates from clocks on the ground, matching the predictions. Together these support the theory of relativity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains both lines of evidence and their support for the theory, but does not analyse the velocities or judge the strength of the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Muons reach the ground in large numbers, and moving atomic clocks keep different time, which supports the theory of relativity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: identifies both lines of evidence and their support for the theory, without explaining the link to time dilation.

dotPoints.description: Account for the origin of cathode rays in a cathode-ray tube

prompts.question: Account for the origin of the cathode rays in a cathode-ray tube, referring to the cathode, the anode and the high voltage between them.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student sets up a low-pressure cathode-ray tube with a heated metal cathode at one end and a metal anode at the other. When the high voltage supply is switched on, a beam travels along the tube and produces a glow where it strikes the glass at the far end.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Accounts for cathode rays as electrons emitted from the heated, negative cathode, and explains that the electric field from the high voltage accelerates them towards the anode
2 marks: Identifies the cathode as the source of the electrons in the rays, without explaining how they are emitted or accelerated
1 mark: Identifies that cathode rays come from the cathode
markerNotes: A strong answer names the cathode as the source and explains that electrons are emitted from its surface.
The high voltage causes the motion: link the electric field between the electrodes to the acceleration of electrons towards the anode.
Say electrons rather than particles in general, since cathode rays are a beam of electrons.
commonStudentErrors: Says the cathode rays are made of protons or positive ions moving from the cathode to the anode.
States that the cathode rays come from the anode or from the glass of the tube.
Describes the rays as light or heat, rather than a beam of electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cathode rays originate at the cathode, the negative electrode of the cathode-ray tube. Electrons are emitted from the heated surface of the cathode. The electric field produced by the high voltage between the cathode and the positively charged anode accelerates these electrons along the tube, so the rays are a beam of electrons travelling towards the anode.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Accounts for the origin of the rays as emitted electrons and explains their acceleration by the electric field, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cathode rays come from the cathode, which emits electrons that travel along the tube towards the anode.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the cathode as the source and the electrons as the rays, but does not explain how the electrons are emitted or accelerated.

sampleAnswers.answer: Cathode rays come from the cathode.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the cathode as the source only.

prompts.question: Analyse how the heated cathode, the anode and the high voltage between them work together to produce cathode rays, and why the tube must be at low pressure for the rays to form a beam.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A physics teacher shows a glass cathode-ray tube with most of the air pumped out. A heated metal cathode sits at one end, a metal anode with a small hole in its centre sits near the other, and a high voltage is applied between them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the heated cathode emits electrons that the electric field from the high voltage accelerates through the hole in the anode, and explains that low pressure lets the electrons travel the length of the tube with few collisions
5 marks: Analyses the roles of the cathode, anode and high voltage in producing the rays, with some explanation of why low pressure is needed
4 marks: Describes how the electrodes and high voltage produce electrons that move towards the anode, with a limited reason for the low pressure
3 marks: Describes that the cathode emits electrons when the high voltage is applied, without explaining the low pressure
2 marks: Identifies the cathode and anode as the electrodes involved in producing the rays
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Link each electrode to its job: the heated cathode emits electrons, and the anode attracts them through its hole.
The high voltage is the cause of acceleration, so state the electric field it creates and its direction.
Explain low pressure in terms of collisions with gas molecules, rather than just naming it.
commonStudentErrors: Says the anode emits the electrons, so the cathode only supports the tube.
States that the rays would form without the high voltage, because they are a natural glow.
Says low pressure makes the electrons faster by pushing them along the tube.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cathode is heated, so electrons are emitted from its surface. The high voltage between the cathode and the anode creates an electric field pointing from the positive anode towards the negative cathode. Electrons are repelled from the cathode and attracted to the anode, so the field accelerates them along the tube. Some pass through the small hole in the anode and form a narrow beam, which is the cathode ray. The gas in the tube is at low pressure, so there are few gas molecules for the electrons to collide with. This means the electrons keep their speed and direction over the length of the cathode-ray tube, so the beam can reach the far end and be observed. Both the cathode and the high voltage are essential, since removing either one stops the rays.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the electrodes, the field and the low pressure together, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The heated cathode emits electrons, and the high voltage pulls them towards the positive anode to form a beam. The low pressure means the electrons are not slowed much by gas molecules, so the beam can reach the far end of the tube.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the roles of the cathode and high voltage, with a brief reason for the low pressure, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The cathode and anode are the electrodes that produce the rays.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the electrodes only, without the role of the high voltage or the pressure.

dotPoints.description: Describe the observations made inside a low-pressure tube when a cathode ray interacts with a Maltese cross, a paddle wheel, electric fields, and magnetic fields

prompts.question: Describe the observations made inside the low-pressure tube when the cathode rays strike a Maltese cross and a paddle wheel placed in the beam path.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student uses a low-pressure tube with a fluorescent screen at one end. First a metal Maltese cross is placed in the beam path, and then a small paddle wheel mounted on rails is placed in the beam path.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the sharp shadow of the Maltese cross on the screen and the paddle wheel rolling along its rails, explaining that the rays travel in straight lines and carry momentum
2 marks: Describes both observations without explaining what they show about the cathode rays
1 mark: Identifies one observation made in the tube
markerNotes: Describe what is seen or happens, such as a sharp shadow or a rolling wheel, not only the names of the apparatus.
Link the shadow to straight-line travel and the rolling wheel to the rays carrying momentum.
Keep the two observations separate so the marker can credit each one.
commonStudentErrors: Says the screen is lit up where the cross is, rather than dark where the shadow falls.
States that the paddle wheel is pushed by the glass of the tube rather than by the rays.
Says the cross stops the rays from existing instead of casting a shadow.

sampleAnswers.answer: Inside the low-pressure tube, the Maltese cross casts a sharp shadow on the fluorescent screen, which shows that cathode rays travel in straight lines and are blocked by the metal. The paddle wheel rolls along its rails, away from the cathode, which shows that the rays carry momentum and transfer it to the paddles when they strike them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both observations and explains the straight-line travel and momentum, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: A shadow of the Maltese cross appears on the screen. The paddle wheel rolls along the track.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both observations accurately but does not explain what they show.

sampleAnswers.answer: A shadow of the Maltese cross appears on the screen.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one observation only.

prompts.question: Analyse the observations when the cathode rays pass between charged plates and then through a magnetic field, and explain what these observations show about the charge of the rays.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: In a low-pressure tube, a pair of charged metal plates sits either side of the beam, with the upper plate positive. When the plates are switched on, the beam bends upwards towards the positive plate. A separate magnet then applies a magnetic field at right angles to the beam, and the beam curves.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the upward deflection towards the positive plate and the curved path in the magnetic field, linking both to a negative charge and to the rays moving as particles
5 marks: Analyses both deflections, linking them to a negative charge, with some detail on the direction of the forces
4 marks: Describes the deflections in the electric and magnetic fields, with a link to the charge of the rays
3 marks: Describes the deflection in one of the fields, with some reference to the charge of the rays
2 marks: Identifies that the beam is deflected by an electric or magnetic field
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Describe each deflection by direction: towards the positive plate in the electric field, and curved in the magnetic field.
Link attraction to a positive plate with negative charge, and a force at right angles to the field and velocity with motion.
Keep the electric and magnetic effects separate before drawing the combined conclusion.
commonStudentErrors: Says the rays are deflected towards the negative plate, which contradicts the observation.
States that the magnetic field speeds up the rays, rather than deflecting them.
Concludes that the rays are positively charged because they move in a magnetic field.

sampleAnswers.answer: When the plates are switched on, the beam bends upwards towards the positive plate. This shows that the rays are attracted to positive charge, so they must carry negative charge. The electric field exerts a force on each ray towards the positive plate, so the path curves. When the magnet applies a magnetic field at right angles to the beam, the beam curves again, in a direction set by the field and the direction of travel. A magnetic force acts only on moving charges, so this deflection shows the rays are moving charged particles. Together the two deflections show that cathode rays are negatively charged particles in motion, and that both the electric field and the magnetic field act on them. Neither deflection would occur for a neutral beam or for light, so the evidence points to a stream of charged particles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses both deflections and links them to a negative charge in motion, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The beam bends towards the positive plate, so the rays are negatively charged. The magnetic field also bends the beam, which shows that the rays are moving charges.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both deflections with a link to charge, but does not explain the direction of the forces, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The beam is deflected by the electric field between the plates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one deflection without any link to charge.

dotPoints.description: Analyse how observations of cathode rays provide evidence that cathode rays consist of particles with mass and charge

prompts.question: Assess the contribution of the results of these experiments in developing an understanding of the existence and properties of electrons.
markerNotes: Assess means judge how far the results support the claims, not only describe them.
A top answer covers both the existence of electrons, as charged particles, and their properties, such as mass and charge-to-mass ratio.
Name the experiment and the observation it gives, then say what that shows about electrons.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the cathode-ray tube without saying what any result shows about electrons.
Covers only the existence of electrons, or only their properties, and so cannot reach the top rows.
Treats the charge-to-mass ratio as measured directly, without the electric and magnetic field results that gave it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Provides a comprehensive assessment of the experimental results; Relates the results to both existence and properties of electrons
4 marks: Provides a sound assessment of the experimental results; Relates the results to the properties and/or existence of electrons
3 marks: Outlines an experiment and/or results; Relates experimental results to the existence and/or properties of electrons
2 marks: Outlines a relevant experiment or result; OR; Relates an experimental result to the existence or property of electrons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Experimental results and their interpretation have played an essential role in developing and understanding of both the existence and properties of electrons.
It was demonstrated that cathode rays could be deflected by an electric field in a manner consistent with negatively charged particles. This experiment also allowed the deduction that the cathode rays were not electromagnetic waves because the latter would not be deflected by an electric field.
The combined effect of changing the magnitudes of electric and magnetic fields through which the electrons passed was measured and from this the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron was calculated.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: the answer assesses the deflection results for both the existence of electrons (charged particles, not waves) and their properties, including the charge-to-mass ratio from the combined fields. The middle answer outlines a result and links it to charge, but does not assess its strength or cover mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thomson's cathode-ray tube showed that cathode rays are deflected by an electric field, so they carry negative charge. This supports the view that the rays are charged particles, which are electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row by outlining an experiment and its result, and relating it to the existence of electrons. It does not assess how strongly the results support the claim, and it covers neither the mass of the electron nor its charge-to-mass ratio. Adding the combined-field result and the charge-to-mass ratio would lift it towards the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrons were found through cathode-ray experiments.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving some relevant information about the period and cathode rays. It describes no experiment or result, and naming the deflection experiment and its result would lift it to the 2-mark row.

dotPoints.description: Explain how the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron was first determined

prompts.question: Outline how Thomson used an electric field and a magnetic field to determine the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student reads about an early experiment in which a beam of cathode rays passes through a region containing an electric field and a magnetic field, both at right angles to the beam and to each other.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines how the electric and magnetic forces are balanced to establish the speed of the electrons, then how the circular path in the magnetic field gives the charge-to-mass ratio
2 marks: Outlines how balancing the electric and magnetic forces gives the speed of the electrons, without linking this to the charge-to-mass ratio
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: The key idea is balance: equal and opposite electric and magnetic forces leave the beam undeflected, which gives the speed.
The ratio comes from the radius of the circular path in the magnetic field, not from the balance step alone.
Give the order of the steps, since removing the electric field is what allows the circular path to be measured.
commonStudentErrors: Says the charge-to-mass ratio was found by weighing a single electron.
Says the electric field alone bends the beam into a circle, so the ratio comes from the electric field only.
Says the beam is undeflected because the tube contains no fields.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thomson adjusted the electric and magnetic fields until their forces on the beam balanced, so the beam was undeflected. This gave the speed of the electrons. He then removed the electric field, leaving the magnetic field to bend the beam into a circular path. Measuring the radius of this path, together with the speed and the field strength, gave the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the balance step and the circular path, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thomson balanced the electric and magnetic forces so the beam was undeflected, which gave the speed of the electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the speed step only, without the circular path that gives the ratio.

sampleAnswers.answer: Thomson used an electric field and a magnetic field on a beam of electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information about the fields but not how the ratio was found.

prompts.question: Analyse what Thomson's results for the charge-to-mass ratio, obtained with different cathode metals and gases, suggested about the particles in cathode rays and about atoms.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares results from several cathode-ray tubes. Each tube has a different metal cathode and contains a different gas at low pressure, yet the charge-to-mass ratio measured for the particles is the same in every tube.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses that the same ratio from different cathode metals and gases implies a particle common to all atoms, and that its very large ratio shows it is far lighter than any atom
5 marks: Analyses the constant ratio across different metals and gases as evidence for a particle common to all atoms, with limited reference to its mass
4 marks: Describes the constant ratio found with different metals and gases, and links it to particles present in all atoms
3 marks: Describes that the ratio was the same in different tubes, with some link to the particles
2 marks: Identifies that the charge-to-mass ratio was constant across the tubes
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Use the variation in cathode metals and gases as the key evidence: a constant result means the particle is common to all atoms.
Link the very large charge-to-mass ratio to a very small mass, rather than just stating that the ratio is large.
Conclude that atoms have internal structure, which challenged the idea that atoms are indivisible.
commonStudentErrors: Says the charge-to-mass ratio changed with the gas, so the particles come from the gas.
States that Thomson weighed the electron and found its mass directly.
Says the results show that electrons were found in the nucleus of atoms.

sampleAnswers.answer: The same charge-to-mass ratio was found with different cathode metals and different gases, so the particles in cathode rays cannot come from one particular metal or gas. They must be a common part of the matter in every tube, and so of all atoms. The ratio was also very large, which means the particles have far less mass than any atom known at the time. Thomson concluded that these particles, now known as electrons, are a fundamental part of atoms, and that atoms are not indivisible. This was a key step towards the idea that atoms have internal structure. Because the same particle appeared in every tube, it could be treated as a universal building block, which challenged the view that atoms are indivisible and opened the way to later models of atomic structure.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the constant ratio and what it implies about mass and structure, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ratio was the same for different cathode metals and gases, so the particles are not from one metal or gas. The ratio was very large, so the particles must be much lighter than atoms, which suggests they are part of every atom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the constant ratio and its implication for mass, with a link to atoms, which meets the 4-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The charge-to-mass ratio was the same in each tube.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the constant result but does not explain what it shows.
