dotPoints.description: Analyse how experimental evidence can lead to refinements in scientific models

prompts.question: Outline how experimental evidence about the fine structure of spectral lines led to a refinement of the Bohr model.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is told that when the spectral lines of hydrogen were examined with more precise instruments, each line was found to be made of several closely spaced lines.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the experimental evidence of fine structure in spectral lines, and how elliptical orbits were added to the Bohr model as a refinement, showing how evidence can refine a model
2 marks: Outlines the experimental evidence that the Bohr model could not explain, without the refinement
1 mark: Identifies a new observation about spectral lines
markerNotes: Name the evidence precisely: the fine structure, where each spectral line is split into closely spaced lines.
Describe the refinement: elliptical orbits added to the Bohr model, rather than a new model replacing it.
Use the phrase experimental evidence, since the question asks how evidence leads to refinement.
commonStudentErrors: Says the Bohr model was replaced entirely by elliptical orbits, which were a new model.
States that fine structure was predicted by the Bohr model before it was measured.
Says spectral lines are split because electrons were discovered inside the nucleus.

sampleAnswers.answer: Higher-precision measurements showed that each of the spectral lines was made of several closely spaced lines, a fine structure the Bohr model could not predict. This experimental evidence led Sommerfeld to refine the model by allowing elliptical orbits as well as circular ones. The refinement kept the core ideas of the Bohr model while improving its agreement with observations. This shows how experimental evidence can lead to refinement of a scientific model rather than its replacement.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the fine-structure evidence and how elliptical orbits refined the model, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Measurements showed that spectral lines were split, which the Bohr model could not explain.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the evidence but not the refinement that followed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Higher-precision measurements showed new detail in spectral lines.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a new observation only.

prompts.question: Analyse how the discovery that spectral lines have fine structure, and the Bohr model's failure to explain it, led scientists to refine the model rather than abandon it, and why some evidence refines a model while other evidence replaces it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares two historical cases: the refinement of the Bohr model after fine structure was observed, and the replacement of the plum pudding model after the gold foil experiment.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how fine structure evidence refined the Bohr model by keeping its core idea, and contrasts this with the replacement of the plum pudding model, showing why evidence can refine or replace a model
5 marks: Analyses how fine structure evidence led to a refinement of the Bohr model, with limited reference to replacement
4 marks: Describes a refinement of a model by new evidence, with a comparison to a model that was replaced
3 marks: Describes the fine structure evidence and the Bohr model's response to it
2 marks: Identifies that experimental evidence can lead to a refinement of a model
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Analyse the reason for the outcome: a refinement keeps the core idea, while a replacement comes from evidence the core idea cannot survive.
Use both cases: the Bohr model refined by fine structure, and the plum pudding model replaced after the gold foil experiment.
End by stating the general principle, not just listing two examples.
commonStudentErrors: Says the Bohr model was discarded when fine structure was found.
States that every new observation replaces a scientific model completely.
Says the plum pudding model was refined by the gold foil results rather than replaced.

sampleAnswers.answer: Experimental evidence can lead to refinement when new observations can be explained by modifying a model's existing ideas. The Bohr model explained the main hydrogen spectrum, but precise measurements showed that spectral lines have fine structure, which the model could not predict. Because the basic idea of quantised energy levels still explained most of the data, scientists modified the model rather than abandoning it. Sommerfeld allowed elliptical as well as circular orbits, and later relativistic effects were added, which produced the fine structure and kept the Bohr model's core. This is a refinement of the Bohr model. By contrast, the plum pudding model was replaced after the gold foil experiment, because its basic picture of a spread-out positive charge could not account for large-angle scattering. So new evidence refines a model when the core idea survives, and replaces it when the core idea fails the test. This distinction shows how the same kind of evidence can lead to different outcomes in scientific models.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses why the same kind of evidence refines one model and replaces another, using both cases, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sommerfeld refined the Bohr model with elliptical orbits to explain the fine structure of spectral lines, keeping its core idea. The plum pudding model was replaced after the gold foil experiment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes a refinement and a replacement as two cases, without analysing why the outcomes differ, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Experimental evidence led to a refinement of the Bohr model.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the refinement without the fine structure evidence or the analysis.

dotPoints.description: Relate the isotopic mass number of an element to its subatomic components

prompts.question: Outline how the mass number of an isotope relates to the number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus, and why electrons contribute very little to it.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is given two isotopes of carbon, both with six protons, but with different mass numbers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines that the mass number is the total of protons and neutrons in an isotope's nucleus, that isotopes differ in neutron number, and that electrons contribute negligibly
2 marks: Outlines the mass number as the total of protons and neutrons, without the isotope or electron points
1 mark: Identifies a component of the nucleus that counts towards the mass number
markerNotes: Relate the mass number to the nucleus: it counts protons and neutrons, which are the nucleons.
Explain why isotopes have different mass numbers: the same protons, but different neutrons.
Give the electron point: electrons are much lighter, so they are excluded from the mass number.
commonStudentErrors: Says the mass number includes the electrons, so isotopes differ by their electrons.
States that isotopes have different numbers of protons, which changes the mass number.
Says the mass number is the number of electrons in an atom.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass number of an isotope is the total number of protons and neutrons in its nucleus, which together are called nucleons. Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. Electrons contribute very little to the mass number because they are much lighter than protons and neutrons, so they are not counted in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relates the mass number to the protons and neutrons, explains isotopes, and why electrons are excluded, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass number is the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Relates the mass number to the nucleons without explaining isotopes or electrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass number includes the protons in the nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one component only.

prompts.question: Distinguish between two isotopes of the same element and two different elements that have the same mass number, using their protons and neutrons.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student compares carbon-12 and carbon-14, which are isotopes of carbon, with nitrogen-14 and carbon-14, which share the same mass number of 14.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes isotopes by their differing neutron numbers with the same protons, and distinguishes different elements with the same mass number by their differing protons, using specific examples
4 marks: Distinguishes isotopes and elements with the same mass number, with reference to protons and neutrons
3 marks: Describes the protons and neutrons of isotopes, with some reference to the element
2 marks: Identifies that isotopes have different mass numbers and the same protons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Distinguish means state the difference, not just describe both: isotopes differ in neutrons, while elements differ in protons.
Use the mass number to show what is shared: nitrogen-14 and carbon-14 share mass number 14 but not the element.
Give examples with proton and neutron counts, such as carbon-12 and carbon-14.
commonStudentErrors: Says isotopes have different numbers of protons, which is why they are different isotopes.
States that nitrogen-14 and carbon-14 are isotopes because they have the same mass number.
Says the same mass number means the nuclei have identical protons and neutrons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons, which fixes the element, but different numbers of neutrons, which gives different mass numbers. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, but carbon-14 has eight neutrons, so its mass number is larger. Nitrogen-14 and carbon-14 share the same mass number of 14, but nitrogen has seven protons while carbon has six. They are therefore different elements, and the equal mass number only shows that both nuclei contain the same total number of nucleons. This is why the mass number alone cannot identify an element. The number of protons decides which element a nucleus belongs to, while the number of neutrons distinguishes one isotope from another.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes isotopes by neutron number and different elements by protons, with examples, which meets the 5-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes, with the same six protons but different numbers of neutrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Distinguishes the isotopes by neutron number, but does not compare them with a different element, which meets the 2-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Isotopes have different mass numbers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Provides relevant information only.

dotPoints.description: Describe the range and effect of the strong nuclear force on nucleons

prompts.question: Describe the range of the strong nuclear force and its effect on nucleons inside a nucleus.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is comparing the forces acting inside a nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons packed closely together.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the strong nuclear force as attractive over a very short range of a few femtometres, binding nucleons together and overcoming proton repulsion
2 marks: Describes the strong nuclear force as attractive between nucleons, without its short range
1 mark: Identifies that the strong nuclear force acts inside the nucleus
markerNotes: Give the range as a few femtometres, and state that the force is negligible beyond it.
Describe the effect on nucleons: binding them, which counters electrostatic repulsion between protons.
Link range to effect: the force only holds nucleons that are close together.
commonStudentErrors: Says the strong nuclear force acts over long distances, like gravity.
States that the strong nuclear force only acts on protons, not neutrons.
Says the strong nuclear force pushes nucleons apart in the nucleus.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force acts only over a very short range, a few femtometres, which is about the size of a nucleus. Within this range it is attractive and binds protons and neutrons, which are collectively called nucleons, together. Its effect is to hold the nucleus together by overcoming the electrostatic repulsion between protons. Beyond this short range, the strong nuclear force has no significant effect on nucleons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the short range, the attraction between nucleons and its effect on the nucleus, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force is attractive and holds nucleons together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the attraction and effect without the short range.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force acts inside the nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a location only.

prompts.question: Analyse why the strong nuclear force, with its short range, acts equally on protons and neutrons, and explain what this implies about the size of a stable nucleus.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student notes that the strong nuclear force does not distinguish between protons and neutrons, and that very heavy nuclei tend to be unstable.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses that the strong force acts equally on protons and neutrons but only over short range, so binding saturates and the repulsion between protons limits stable nuclear size, with neutrons needed for stability
5 marks: Analyses the equal action and short range of the strong force, with some reasoning about the size of nuclei
4 marks: Describes the equal action on protons and neutrons and the short range of the force, with a link to nucleus size
3 marks: Describes the short range of the strong force and its effect on nearby nucleons
2 marks: Identifies that the strong force acts on both protons and neutrons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Explain the two properties separately, then combine them: equal action explains why neutrons also bind, and short range limits the size of a nucleus.
Connect short range with nuclear size: each nucleon only interacts with its neighbours.
Note that repulsion acts over the whole nucleus, which is why neutrons become necessary for stability.
commonStudentErrors: Says the strong nuclear force acts only on protons, so neutrons are not bound.
States that the strong nuclear force has a long range, so large nuclei are easily held together.
Says the size of a stable nucleus is limited by the electrons orbiting it.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force is charge-independent: it attracts a proton to a neighbouring proton, a proton to a neutron, and a neutron to a neutron with roughly the same strength, so protons and neutrons are bound equally. Its short range means that each nucleon only attracts those immediately next to it, not every nucleon in the nucleus. As a nucleus gets larger, a nucleon at its centre is surrounded by many others and gains little extra binding from distant nucleons. Meanwhile, the electrostatic repulsion between protons acts over the whole nucleus, so it grows with the number of protons. Stable nuclei therefore need proportionally more neutrons, which add strong attraction without adding repulsion. Eventually the repulsion from many protons outweighs what the short-range strong force can hold, which limits the size of a stable nucleus. This is why very heavy nuclei tend to be unstable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the equal action and short range of the strong force and what they imply for the size of a stable nucleus, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force acts on protons and neutrons equally. Its short range means it only binds nearby nucleons, so very large nuclei are difficult to hold together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the equal action and short range, with a link to nucleus size, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force acts on both protons and neutrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the equal action without the range or the implication for size.

dotPoints.description: Explain how the balance between the strong nuclear force and the electrostatic repulsion force impacts the stability of the nucleus

prompts.question: Explain how the balance between the strong nuclear force and electrostatic repulsion affects whether a nucleus is stable.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is comparing a small, stable nucleus with a very large nucleus containing many protons.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that stability depends on the strong nuclear force balancing electrostatic repulsion between protons, that nuclei become unstable when repulsion dominates, and that neutrons add attraction without repulsion
2 marks: Identifies the strong nuclear force and electrostatic repulsion, and that their balance affects stability, without explaining how
1 mark: Identifies that the strong nuclear force holds nucleons together
markerNotes: Explain the balance as the cause of stability: the two forces must be matched, so neither dominates.
Use the case of very large nuclei, where repulsion from many protons outweighs the short-range attraction.
Link neutrons to stability: they add strong attraction without adding repulsion.
commonStudentErrors: Says the nucleus is stable because protons repel each other less when there are more of them.
States that electrostatic repulsion holds the nucleus together, and the strong force pushes it apart.
Says the strong nuclear force only acts between electrons and protons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrostatic repulsion between the protons pushes the nucleus apart, while the strong nuclear force attracts all the nucleons together. When these two forces are in balance, the nucleus shows stability. In very large nuclei, the repulsion between many protons becomes too great for the short-range strong nuclear force to hold, and the nucleus becomes unstable and may decay. Adding neutrons increases the strong attraction without adding repulsion, which helps restore the balance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains that stability depends on the balance of the two forces, what happens when repulsion dominates, and the role of neutrons, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Electrostatic repulsion pushes a nucleus apart, while the strong nuclear force holds it together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies both forces without explaining how their balance determines stability.

sampleAnswers.answer: The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one force and its effect only.

prompts.question: Analyse why the neutron-to-proton ratio of stable nuclei tends to increase as nuclei become larger, using the balance between the strong nuclear force and electrostatic repulsion.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student examines a graph of stable nuclei and notices that heavier stable nuclei contain noticeably more neutrons than protons, while light stable nuclei have roughly equal numbers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses why the long-range electrostatic repulsion between protons grows faster than the short-range strong attraction, so extra neutrons are needed to restore stability, up to a limit beyond which no stable nuclei exist
5 marks: Analyses the balance of the two forces as nuclei grow, with some reasoning about why neutrons restore stability
4 marks: Describes the neutron-to-proton ratio of stable nuclei and links the extra neutrons to the balance with repulsion
3 marks: Describes the neutron-to-proton pattern of stable nuclei, with some reference to the strong nuclear force
2 marks: Identifies that heavier stable nuclei contain more neutrons than protons
1 mark: Provides some relevant information
markerNotes: Compare the ranges: electrostatic repulsion is long range and the strong force is short range, so the balance shifts as nuclei grow.
Explain how neutrons help: they add strong attraction without adding repulsion.
Finish with the limit: no stable nuclei exist beyond a certain size.
commonStudentErrors: Says heavier nuclei have more neutrons because neutrons are heavier than protons.
States that the strong nuclear force grows with the number of protons, so heavier nuclei need fewer neutrons.
Says the balance is between electrons and neutrons in the nucleus.

sampleAnswers.answer: For light nuclei, the number of neutrons is roughly equal to the number of protons, and the strong nuclear force easily balances the electrostatic repulsion between the protons. As nuclei become larger, the number of protons increases, and the electrostatic repulsion acts between every pair of protons across the whole nucleus. Its long range means that its total effect grows faster than the short-range strong attraction, which acts only between neighbouring nucleons. To maintain stability, extra neutrons are added: each neutron adds strong nuclear attraction to its neighbours without adding any electrostatic repulsion, so it helps restore the balance. The neutron-to-proton ratio therefore increases with size. Beyond a certain size, however, even the largest possible excess of neutrons cannot restore the balance, so no stable nuclei exist and heavy nuclei decay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses why the neutron-to-proton ratio rises with size, using the long-range repulsion and short-range attraction, which meets the 6-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Light nuclei have about equal numbers of neutrons and protons. Heavier nuclei need more neutrons, because neutrons add strong attraction without adding repulsion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the change in the ratio and gives a reason based on neutrons, which meets the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Heavier stable nuclei have more neutrons than protons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the pattern without explaining the balance of forces.

dotPoints.description: Describe the process of alpha decay, beta decay and gamma decay

prompts.question: Describe the process of alpha decay and the process of gamma decay in an unstable nucleus.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class is shown two sealed radioactive sources, one that emits alpha particles and one that emits gamma rays, and is asked what happens inside each nucleus.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes alpha decay as an unstable nucleus emitting a helium-4 particle that lowers both the mass number and atomic number, and gamma decay as a nucleus in an excited state emitting a photon with no change in composition
2 marks: Describes one of the decays accurately and identifies the radiation emitted in the other
1 mark: Identifies the radiation emitted in alpha decay or gamma decay
markerNotes: Name the particle or radiation in each decay, then describe what happens to the nucleus.
State whether the mass number and atomic number change, since this separates alpha decay from gamma decay.
Explain that gamma decay releases energy from an excited nucleus rather than changing its composition.
commonStudentErrors: Says gamma decay changes the element, because the nucleus loses energy.
Describes alpha decay as the emission of an electron, which confuses it with beta decay.
Identifies gamma decay as the emission of particles with mass.

sampleAnswers.answer: In alpha decay, an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle, a helium-4 nucleus made of two protons and two neutrons, so its mass number and atomic number both fall. In gamma decay, a nucleus in an excited state drops to a lower energy state and emits a gamma ray, a high-energy photon. Neither the mass number nor the atomic number changes in gamma decay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes both decays, the change in the nucleus for alpha decay and the unchanged composition for gamma decay.

sampleAnswers.answer: In alpha decay, an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle made of two protons and two neutrons. In gamma decay, the nucleus releases a gamma ray.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes alpha decay accurately and identifies the radiation in gamma decay, without the change in the nucleus.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha decay emits an alpha particle, and gamma decay emits a gamma ray.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the radiation in each decay without describing the nucleus.

prompts.question: Distinguish between alpha decay, beta decay and gamma decay to show why the student's claim is incorrect.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student claims that alpha, beta and gamma radiation all come from the same process inside a nucleus, because all three are emitted by radioactive sources.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes all three decays by what is emitted and by how the nucleus changes, and explains why this shows the claim is incorrect
4 marks: Distinguishes the three decays by what is emitted, with a clear reference to the change in the nucleus in at least two of them
3 marks: Describes what is emitted in each decay, with limited reference to the change in the nucleus
2 marks: Identifies the radiation emitted in at least one of the decays
1 mark: Provides a minimal relevant response about radioactive decay
markerNotes: Answer the claim directly first, then distinguish the three decays one at a time.
Give the change to the nucleus for each decay, not only the particle that is emitted.
Use the word emitted for each radiation and say which change inside the nucleus produces it.
commonStudentErrors: States that all three radiations come from the same process because they are all emitted by radioactive sources.
Describes gamma decay as a change of the nucleus into a different element.
Says beta decay emits a proton, rather than an electron and an antineutrino.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha decay, beta decay and gamma decay are different processes, so the student's claim is incorrect. In alpha decay, an unstable nucleus emits an alpha particle made of two protons and two neutrons, so the nucleus loses two units of atomic number and becomes a different element. In beta decay, a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton, and an electron and an antineutrino are emitted, so the atomic number rises by one while the mass number is unchanged. In gamma decay, a nucleus in an excited state drops to a lower energy state and emits a gamma ray, so its composition does not change. The three processes differ in what is emitted and in how the nucleus changes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: distinguishes all three decays by what is emitted and by the change in the nucleus, and rejects the claim with reasons.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha decay emits an alpha particle, which lowers the atomic number of the nucleus. Beta decay emits an electron, and gamma decay emits a photon, so the three processes are different.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes what is emitted in each decay, with limited reference to the change in the nucleus.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha decay, beta decay and gamma decay emit different radiation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: a general relevant statement that does not distinguish the decays.

dotPoints.description: Compare the composition, charge, mass, ionising ability, and penetration of alpha radiation, beta radiation and gamma radiation

prompts.question: Outline TWO methods that could be used to determine which source is the alpha emitter, and which source is the beta emitter.
markerNotes: Each method needs the observation that tells the sources apart, such as a smaller drop in count for beta than for alpha through the same material.
Two methods are required, and they must be different tests. Describing what alpha and beta particles are earns no method marks.
Deflection in a magnetic field separates the sources because alpha and beta particles carry opposite charges, so they bend in opposite directions.
commonStudentErrors: Describes what alpha and beta particles are without giving a method to tell the sources apart.
Gives two versions of the same test, such as two checks with paper, so only one method is really outlined.
States a difference, such as "the count drops", without saying which source it identifies.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines TWO methods and subsequent observations that could be used to identify each source as either alpha or beta emitters
2 marks: Outlines a method that could be used to distinguish the sources; OR; Identifies TWO methods that could be used to identify each source
1 mark: Provides some relevant information

sampleAnswers.answer:
Pass the radiation through a thin material to a detector. Observe any changes in counts. The beta source count will be reduced by an amount less than the alpha source count.
Pass each type of radiation through a magnetic field and observe any differences in deflection and observe deflection in opposite directions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row with two methods, each with the observation that tells the sources apart: penetration through a thin material and deflection in a magnetic field. A middle answer names the method but leaves out the identifying observation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Test each source in a magnetic field. Direct a narrow beam through the field and record where it strikes a detector, so the deflection of each source can be compared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row by outlining a method that could distinguish the sources: “Test each source in a magnetic field”. No observation says which source is alpha and which is beta, so neither source is identified. Stating the direction of deflection for each source would lift it to the 3-mark row.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha particles are positive helium nuclei; beta particles are electrons.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row by giving relevant information about the two radiations, but it describes no method. Naming a test and the result that separates the sources would lift it to the 2-mark row.

prompts.scenario: A scientist has two unlabelled sources of radiation. One source emits alpha particles and the other emits beta particles.
prompts.hscSection: Section II (80 marks). Attempt Questions 21–36. Allow about 2 hours and 25 minutes for this section.

dotPoints.description: Use nuclear decay equations to describe reactions, including radioactive decay and transmutation

prompts.question: Explain what a nuclear decay equation shows about radioactive decay and transmutation, including what the superscript and subscript represent.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is given a nuclear decay equation with the parent nucleus on the left and the daughter nucleus and an emitted particle on the right.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that a nuclear decay equation records a parent nucleus changing into a daughter nucleus and an emitted particle, and that the superscript and subscript give the mass number and atomic number
2 marks: Describes the parent and daughter nuclei and the emitted particle, with limited reference to transmutation
1 mark: Identifies that a nuclear decay equation shows a nucleus changing
markerNotes: State what the arrow shows: the parent nucleus changes into the daughter nucleus and the emitted particle.
Name the superscript as the mass number and the subscript as the atomic number, rather than calling either one the element.
Link transmutation to a change in atomic number, since a change in mass number alone does not make a new element.
commonStudentErrors: Says the superscript is the atomic number and the subscript is the mass number.
Describes transmutation as any decay, even when the element does not change.

sampleAnswers.answer: A nuclear decay equation shows a parent nucleus changing into a daughter nucleus and an emitted particle. In radioactive decay the parent is unstable and the equation records the new nucleus. Transmutation occurs when the atomic number changes, so the daughter is a different element. The superscript gives the mass number, the total of protons and neutrons, and the subscript gives the atomic number, the number of protons, which identifies the element.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: explains what the equation records and what the superscript and subscript give, with transmutation linked to atomic number.

sampleAnswers.answer: A nuclear decay equation shows a parent nucleus changing into a daughter nucleus and an emitted particle, so the element can change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the nuclei and the emitted particle, with limited reference to transmutation.

sampleAnswers.answer: A nuclear decay equation shows the parent and daughter nuclei and the emitted particle.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies what the equation shows without explaining the notation.

prompts.question: Apply the meaning of a nuclear decay equation to a chain of decays, explaining how each step transmutes the parent into a different element until a stable nucleus is produced.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A radioactive isotope undergoes alpha decay to form a daughter nucleus, which then undergoes beta decay to form a stable nucleus.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies nuclear decay equations to each step, showing transmutation to a different element and conservation of mass number and atomic number, and identifies the final stable nucleus
4 marks: Applies the equations to each step and shows that the element changes, with some reference to conservation
3 marks: Describes the alpha and beta decay steps and the new nuclei they form, with limited reference to transmutation
2 marks: Identifies that each decay produces a new nucleus
1 mark: Provides a minimal relevant response about radioactive decay
markerNotes: Trace the chain one step at a time, stating the particle emitted and the change to the element in each step.
Use conservation of mass number and atomic number to show that each equation balances.
State that the chain ends at a stable nucleus, which no longer decays.
commonStudentErrors: Treats the daughter nucleus as the same element as the parent after alpha decay.
States that a stable nucleus can still decay further in the chain.

sampleAnswers.answer: Each step of radioactive decay can be written as a nuclear decay equation, which shows the parent nucleus changing into a daughter nucleus and an emitted particle. In the first step, alpha decay emits an alpha particle, so the atomic number falls and the nucleus becomes a different element, which is transmutation. The daughter nucleus then undergoes beta decay, in which a neutron becomes a proton and an electron and an antineutrino are emitted, so the atomic number rises. Each equation balances, with the same total mass number and total atomic number on both sides. The chain therefore traces the transmutation from the original parent to a stable nucleus, and it ends there because the stable nucleus does not decay further.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: applies the equations step by step, shows transmutation and conservation, and identifies the stable end point.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha decay forms a daughter nucleus that is a different element. Beta decay then changes that daughter again, and the final nucleus is stable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes the two steps and the new nuclei, with limited reference to transmutation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Alpha decay and beta decay each produce a new nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: a minimal statement about the decays.

dotPoints.description: Apply conservation of mass, energy and charge to nuclear reactions, transmutation and radioactive decay

prompts.question: Demonstrate how conservation of charge applies to radioactive decay, using beta decay as an example.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student's notes show a beta decay in which the nucleus changes but the emitted electron is not recorded.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Demonstrates conservation of charge with a specific decay, showing that the charge gained by the daughter nucleus balances the charge of the emitted electron
2 marks: Explains that the negative charge of the emitted electron must be balanced by a change in the nucleus, with limited use of an example
1 mark: Identifies that the total charge is the same before and after a decay
markerNotes: Name the specific decay and say which particle carries the charge, rather than stating the principle alone.
Show the charge balance as the charge of the original nucleus equalling the charge of the daughter nucleus plus the emitted electron.
Explain that the nucleus gains positive charge, which is why the balance works.
commonStudentErrors: States that charge is conserved but does not identify the particle that carries the charge.
Says the daughter nucleus loses positive charge when an electron is emitted.

sampleAnswers.answer: In beta decay, a neutron in the radioactive nucleus changes into a proton, and an electron and an antineutrino are emitted. The daughter nucleus gains one unit of positive charge, which balances the negative charge of the electron. The total charge before and after this radioactive decay is therefore equal, which demonstrates conservation of charge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: demonstrates conservation of charge with a specific decay and shows the balance with the emitted electron.

sampleAnswers.answer: The electron emitted in beta decay has negative charge, so the daughter nucleus must gain positive charge to balance it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: explains the balance through the emitted electron, without a full worked example.

sampleAnswers.answer: The total charge is conserved in beta decay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies conservation without a supporting example.

prompts.question: Apply conservation of charge, nucleon number and energy to this nuclear reaction, explaining what each law requires of the products.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A nitrogen-14 nucleus is struck by an alpha particle, and a proton and an oxygen-17 nucleus are produced.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Applies conservation of charge, nucleon number and energy to the reaction, explaining what each requires of the products and why the alpha particle needs enough kinetic energy
4 marks: Applies conservation of charge and nucleon number to balance the reaction, with some reference to the energy required
3 marks: Describes how charge and nucleon number are conserved across the reaction, with limited reference to energy
2 marks: Identifies that charge is conserved in the reaction
1 mark: Identifies the products of the reaction
markerNotes: Test each law in turn: charge, then nucleon number, then energy, which keeps the answer organised.
State that the total mass-energy, not mass alone, is conserved in a nuclear reaction.
Link the energy requirement to the kinetic energy of the incoming alpha particle.
commonStudentErrors: Says the total mass of the products must equal the total mass of the reactants exactly, ignoring the energy involved.
States that charge is conserved because the alpha particle is positive, without comparing the totals on each side.

sampleAnswers.answer: This reaction is a transmutation, because the nitrogen nucleus becomes a different element. Conservation of charge requires the total charge of the products to equal the total charge of the reactants, so the alpha particle and the nitrogen nucleus carry the same positive charge as the proton and the oxygen nucleus together. Conservation of nucleon number requires the total of protons and neutrons to be the same on both sides, so the proton and oxygen-17 nucleus together contain the nucleons of the nitrogen nucleus and the alpha particle. Conservation of energy means the kinetic energy of the incoming alpha particle must supply any energy the nuclear reaction needs, so the alpha particle must carry enough kinetic energy for the reaction to occur.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: applies charge, nucleon number and energy conservation to the reaction, and explains the kinetic energy requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Charge is conserved, since the alpha particle and nitrogen nucleus carry the same total charge as the proton and oxygen nucleus. The alpha particle must also have enough energy for the reaction to occur.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes charge conservation and mentions energy with limited reference to the reaction.

sampleAnswers.answer: The reaction produces a proton and an oxygen nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the products only.

dotPoints.description: Describe the role of the weak force in beta-minus decay and beta-plus transformation

prompts.question: Describe what the weak force changes inside a nucleus during beta-minus decay, and name the particles that are emitted.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student says that the strong nuclear force is responsible for beta-minus decay because it holds the nucleus together.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes the weak force as changing a down quark into an up quark, so a neutron becomes a proton, and names the electron and antineutrino as the particles emitted
2 marks: Describes the weak force as changing a neutron into a proton in beta-minus decay, with limited reference to the particles emitted
1 mark: Identifies the weak force as involved in beta-minus decay
markerNotes: Name the force first, then the quark or nucleon change, then the particles emitted.
Correct the student's idea by stating that the strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together and does not cause the change.
Name the W boson as the mediator of the change, but do not describe it as a particle that is emitted.
commonStudentErrors: Credits the strong nuclear force with causing beta-minus decay because it holds the nucleus together.
Says the weak force emits a neutron, rather than changing a neutron into a proton.

sampleAnswers.answer: In beta-minus decay, the weak force changes a down quark in a neutron into an up quark, so the neutron becomes a proton. The change is mediated by a W boson, which decays into an electron and an antineutrino, and these are the particles emitted from the nucleus. The strong nuclear force only holds the nucleus together, so it is not responsible for this change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes the quark change and names the emitted electron and antineutrino, and corrects the student's idea.

sampleAnswers.answer: The weak force changes a neutron into a proton in beta-minus decay, and an electron is emitted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes the change in beta-minus decay, with limited reference to the particles emitted.

sampleAnswers.answer: The weak force is involved in beta-minus decay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the weak force only.

prompts.question: Distinguish between the role of the weak force in beta-minus decay and in beta-plus transformation, including the change to the nucleus in each case.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class compares a neutron-rich nucleus, which can undergo beta-minus decay, with a proton-rich nucleus, which can undergo beta-plus transformation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Distinguishes the weak force's role in each process by the quark change, the particles emitted and the change in atomic number, and explains why beta-plus transformation needs an energy difference
4 marks: Distinguishes the two processes by the change in nucleons and the particles emitted, with some reference to the weak force
3 marks: Describes the change in a neutron or proton in each process, with limited reference to the weak force
2 marks: Identifies that the weak force changes a neutron or a proton in one of the processes
1 mark: Identifies the weak force as changing one type of nucleon into another
markerNotes: Name the direction of each change first, neutron to proton or proton to neutron, then the particles emitted.
Refer to quarks to show how the weak force changes a nucleon, rather than describing the force in general terms.
Explain that beta-plus transformation needs an energy difference, so it occurs only in proton-rich nuclei.
commonStudentErrors: States that beta-plus transformation turns a neutron into a proton, reversing the direction of beta-minus decay.
Says the strong nuclear force causes both beta-minus decay and beta-plus transformation.

sampleAnswers.answer: In beta-minus decay, the weak force converts a down quark into an up quark, so a neutron becomes a proton, and the nucleus emits an electron and an antineutrino through a W boson. The atomic number increases by one. In beta-plus transformation, the weak force converts an up quark into a down quark, so a proton becomes a neutron, and the nucleus emits a positron and an electron neutrino. The atomic number decreases by one. The beta-plus transformation occurs only when the energy difference between the parent and daughter nuclei is large enough to create the positron, which is why it is found in proton-rich nuclei. In both processes the weak force changes the type of quark, while the strong nuclear force is not involved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: distinguishes the two processes by quark change, emitted particles and atomic number change, and explains the energy requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer: In beta-minus decay, the weak force changes a neutron into a proton. In beta-plus transformation, the weak force changes a proton into a neutron, and a positron is emitted.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes the change in each process, with limited reference to the weak force.

sampleAnswers.answer: The weak force changes one type of nucleon into another.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies the weak force's effect in general terms.

dotPoints.description: Describe the concept of half-life as it relates to a radioisotope

prompts.question: Outline what is meant by the half-life of a radioisotope, and why it does not depend on how many nuclei are in the sample.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A laboratory has a large sample and a small sample of the same radioisotope, and a student asks which sample has the longer half-life.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines half-life as the time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay, and explains that it is a fixed property of the isotope, independent of the number of nuclei
2 marks: Describes half-life as the time for half of the nuclei in a sample to decay, with limited reference to the isotope
1 mark: Identifies half-life as a time associated with radioactive decay
markerNotes: Define half-life in terms of half of the radioactive nuclei, not half of the mass or the sample.
Say that each nucleus decays randomly, so the sample size does not change the half-life.
Name the radioisotope as the thing that has the half-life, because it is a property of each isotope.
commonStudentErrors: Says half-life is the time for all of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
States that a larger sample has a longer half-life because it contains more nuclei.

sampleAnswers.answer: The half-life of a radioisotope is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is a constant property of that isotope, so the large and small samples have the same half-life. Each nucleus decays randomly, with the same probability per unit time, so the number of nuclei present does not change the time taken for half of them to decay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: outlines half-life and explains why it is independent of the number of nuclei.

sampleAnswers.answer: Half-life is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes half-life without the link to the isotope or the independence from sample size.

sampleAnswers.answer: Half-life is a time linked to the decay of a radioisotope.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-mark row: identifies half-life as a time linked to decay.

prompts.question: Discuss how half-life can be used to compare radioisotopes, and why half-life does not predict when any single nucleus will decay.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A technician compares two radioisotopes in storage, one with a short half-life and one with a long half-life, to decide which to use first.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses how half-life compares the stability of radioisotopes, and explains that it describes a large number of nuclei rather than predicting when a single nucleus decays
4 marks: Discusses the use of half-life to compare radioisotopes, with some reference to the random decay of individual nuclei
3 marks: Describes how a shorter or longer half-life shows how quickly a radioisotope decays, with limited discussion of its limits
2 marks: Identifies that half-life can be used to compare radioisotopes
1 mark: Provides a minimal relevant response about the decay of radioisotopes
markerNotes: Compare two radioisotopes explicitly, stating which half-life is shorter and what that implies.
Separate the statement about a large number of nuclei from the statement about a single nucleus.
Use the word random to explain why a single nucleus cannot be predicted from its half-life.
commonStudentErrors: States that a nucleus will decay exactly when its half-life has passed.
Says a radioisotope with a longer half-life always decays faster, reversing the comparison.

sampleAnswers.answer: Half-life can compare radioisotopes because a short half-life means the nuclei decay quickly, so the radioisotope is less stable and its activity falls rapidly, while a long half-life indicates a more stable radioisotope that persists longer. This comparison is valid because half-life is a property of each isotope. However, half-life does not predict when any single nucleus will decay. Decay is random, and each nucleus has the same probability of decaying in a given time, so a single nucleus may decay almost immediately or survive far longer than the half-life. Half-life describes the behaviour of a large number of nuclei, which makes it a statistical measure rather than a prediction for one nucleus.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: discusses half-life as a comparison of stability and explains its statistical limit for a single nucleus.

prompts.question: Analyse how the shapes of two decay curves plotted on the same graph show which radioisotope has the longer half-life.

On this graph, the decay curve for radioisotope A is steeper than that for radioisotope B, so A's amount falls more quickly. The time taken for A's amount to halve is therefore shorter, which means A has the shorter half-life and its nuclei are more likely to decay in any given time. The curve for radioisotope B falls more gradually, so it takes longer to halve and has the longer half-life. The shape of each decay curve, rather than its starting amount, shows which radioisotope decays faster.

dotPoints.description: Relate the decay constant λ to the half-life of radioisotopes

prompts.question: Explain what the decay constant represents, and why a radioisotope with a larger decay constant has a shorter half-life.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is comparing two radioisotopes and is told that one has a much larger decay constant than the other.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that the decay constant is the probability of decay per unit time and that the half-life is inversely proportional to it, so a larger decay constant gives a shorter half-life

markerNotes: Define the decay constant as a probability per unit time, not as a time or a rate of change of mass.

States that a larger decay constant means the radioisotope lasts longer before it decays.

sampleAnswers.answer: The decay constant is the probability per unit time that a nucleus of a radioisotope will decay, and it is constant for that isotope. The half-life is inversely proportional to the decay constant, since the decay constant equals ln 2 divided by the half-life, so a larger decay constant gives a shorter half-life. The radioisotope with the larger decay constant therefore decays faster and halves its amount in less time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: defines the decay constant as a probability per unit time and explains the inverse link to half-life.

sampleAnswers.answer: The decay constant is the probability per unit time of decay, and a larger decay constant means a shorter half-life.

prompts.question: Justify why, for the same number of nuclei, a radioisotope with a larger decay constant emits radiation at a higher rate, and how this relates to its half-life.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two samples contain the same number of nuclei, one of radioisotope X with a large decay constant and one of radioisotope Y with a small decay constant.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies the higher rate of radiation and the shorter half-life of the larger decay constant, linking both to the probability of decay per unit time and to the same number of nuclei

markerNotes: Define the decay constant as a probability per unit time, then build the argument from that single definition.
State the condition, the same number of nuclei, before comparing rates of radiation.

sampleAnswers.answer: The decay constant is the probability per unit time that a single nucleus will decay, so a larger decay constant means each nucleus is more likely to decay in a given time. The two samples contain the same number of nuclei, so the sample with the larger decay constant has more decays in any time interval, and its rate of radiation, or activity, is higher. The same relationship explains the half-life. Because the half-life is inversely proportional to the decay constant, radioisotope X, with the larger decay constant, has the shorter half-life and its amount halves in less time. Radioisotope Y, with the smaller decay constant, has the longer half-life and decays more slowly. The decay constant depends only on the isotope itself, not on temperature, pressure or chemical state, so these differences are fixed properties of each radioisotope.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: justifies the higher rate of radiation and the shorter half-life from the decay constant as a probability per unit time.

prompts.question: Describe how a student could use a physical model in a practical investigation of the radioactive decay of an isotope, and how the results would show its half-life.

commonStudentErrors: Says the coins that land heads up are the ones that decay, which reverses the model.
States that the model gives the exact half-life of a real isotope.

sampleAnswers.answer: In this investigation, a student models radioactive decay with coins that are flipped in rounds. Each coin that lands tails up is removed, representing the random decay of one nucleus. Recording the number of coins left after each round shows the pattern of radioactive decay for the isotope being modelled. The number of rounds needed for half the coins to be removed gives the half-life of the model, which can then be compared with the half-life of the isotope.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: describes the coin model, links random removal to decay, and explains how the counts give the half-life.

prompts.question: Assess the validity of this coin model as a representation of radioactive decay, identifying one limitation and one way the investigation could be improved.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A class uses the same coin model, starting with a large number of coins, and records the count after each round in a table.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the validity of the model by linking random, independent removal to radioactive decay, identifies a specific limitation, and justifies a realistic improvement
5 marks: Assesses the validity of the model with a clear link to random decay and identifies at least one limitation

2 marks: Identifies that the model uses random removal to represent decay
1 mark: Provides a minimal relevant response about the coin model
markerNotes: Judge validity on the features that match, such as random and independent removal, not on how much the coins look like nuclei.
Name a specific limitation, such as discrete rounds replacing continuous time.
Propose an improvement that addresses the limitation you named, such as more coins or repeated trials.
commonStudentErrors: Says the model is valid because it looks like a real isotope.
Lists limitations without linking any of them to the validity of the model.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model is valid in one important respect: each coin has the same chance of being removed in a round, which matches the random and independent decay of each nucleus. The pattern of counts, falling by roughly the same fraction each round, also reflects the exponential pattern of radioactive decay in a sample. The validity of the model therefore rests on its random, independent removal, which is the key feature of radioactive decay. However, the model has a clear limitation: real decay happens in continuous time, whereas the coins are removed in discrete rounds, so the half-life can only be expressed in rounds. A second limitation is that every coin has the same probability, so the model cannot show the different decay constants of different isotopes. One improvement is to use more coins and repeat the investigation several times, averaging the counts to reduce random variation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: assesses validity through the random, independent removal, identifies two limitations, and proposes a justified improvement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The model is valid because each coin has the same chance of being removed, which matches random decay, but it uses rounds rather than continuous time.

dotPoints.description: Outline the contribution of selected scientists to radio-medicine

prompts.question: Outline the contribution of Henri Becquerel and Marie Curie to radio-medicine.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A history display on radio-medicine lists several scientists, and a student is asked to outline the early work of two of them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines Becquerel's discovery of radioactivity and Curie's discovery of radium and polonium with mobile X-ray units, and links each contribution to radio-medicine

sampleAnswers.answer: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896, when uranium salts fogged photographic plates kept in the dark, which opened the study of radiation. Marie Curie then discovered the radioactive elements polonium and radium, and during the First World War she developed mobile X-ray units to image wounded soldiers, an early contribution to radio-medicine.

prompts.question: Discuss how the radioactive tracer technique developed by George de Hevesy and the artificial production of radioisotopes by Frederic and Irene Joliot-Curie each contributed to radio-medicine.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is preparing a timeline of how radioisotopes came to be used in medicine.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses how the tracer technique and the artificial production of radioisotopes each enabled radio-medicine, and explains why the two contributions were needed together
5 marks: Discusses the tracer technique and the artificial production of radioisotopes, with clear links to radio-medicine

1 mark: Provides a minimal relevant response about radioisotopes in medicine
markerNotes: Name each scientist's contribution separately, then connect each one to radio-medicine.
Explain the tracer technique by what it does, following a substance through a living organism.
Explain why both contributions were needed: one showed how to use radioisotopes, and the other supplied them.
commonStudentErrors: Credits Hevesy with discovering radioactivity, which was first identified by Becquerel.

sampleAnswers.answer: George de Hevesy's contribution was the radioactive tracer technique, in which a small amount of a radioisotope is added to a substance so that its movement can be followed. Because the radioisotope emits radiation that can be detected, the tracer shows where a substance goes in a living organism, which underpins many later medical diagnostic methods. Frederic and Irene Joliot-Curie made a different contribution in 1934, when they produced artificial radioisotopes by bombarding aluminium with alpha particles, showing that radioisotopes need not occur naturally. This made it possible to produce radioisotopes in quantity for medical use rather than relying only on natural sources. Together, the tracer technique and the artificial production of radioisotopes established the basis of radio-medicine, because one showed how radioisotopes could be used and the other made them widely available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: discusses both contributions, links each to radio-medicine, and explains why they were needed together.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hevesy developed the radioactive tracer technique to follow substances in organisms. The Joliot-Curies produced artificial radioisotopes for use in medicine.

sampleAnswers.answer: Hevesy and the Joliot-Curies both worked with radioisotopes.

prompts.question: Explain why a gamma-emitting radioisotope with a suitable half-life is used in medical imaging.

sampleAnswers.answer: The suitability of a gamma-emitting radioisotope for medical imaging rests on gamma radiation being penetrating enough to be detected by a camera outside the body. Its half-life must be long enough to complete the scan, but short enough to limit the patient's dose. Its chemical behaviour also allows it to collect in the organ being imaged.

prompts.question: Justify why a short-lived gamma-emitting radioisotope suits a medical scan, while a longer-lived gamma-emitting radioisotope suits an industrial gauge, using the half-life and radiation properties of each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A hospital needs a radioisotope for a scan of a patient, and an engineering firm needs a radioisotope for an industrial gauge that checks the thickness of steel sheet passing through rollers.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies each choice by matching half-life and gamma radiation to the duration and penetration required, and contrasts the medical and industrial requirements in an integrated answer
5 marks: Justifies both choices with reference to half-life and to the penetration of gamma radiation
4 marks: Explains the half-life requirement for each use, with some reference to the radiation type
3 marks: Describes the properties of a suitable radioisotope for the medical scan or the industrial gauge, with limited justification

1 mark: Identifies a radioisotope property relevant to a medical scan or an industrial gauge

sampleAnswers.answer: A short half-life suits a medical scan because the radioisotope must remain active long enough to complete the scan, but decay quickly, so the patient receives only a small dose and the activity falls to a low level soon after. The gamma radiation it emits must also be penetrating enough to leave the body and be detected by a camera, whereas alpha or beta radiation would be absorbed by the body's tissue rather than detected outside it. An industrial gauge needs a longer half-life, so that the source stays active for years and the reading remains steady without frequent replacement. Gamma radiation is again chosen because it penetrates the thick steel sheet, and the amount transmitted through the steel is detected to measure its thickness. The radioisotope is therefore selected for each use by matching its half-life to the required duration and its radiation to the material or body being examined.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: justifies each choice from half-life and penetration, and contrasts the two requirements.

sampleAnswers.answer: The special theory of relativity gives the mass-energy equivalence relationship E = mc². In it, E is energy, m is mass and c is the speed of light in a vacuum, so the energy equivalent of a mass is the mass multiplied by the square of the speed of light. prompts.question: Discuss what the mass-energy equivalence relationship shows about the nature of mass, and why mass can act as a store of energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass-energy equivalence relationship shows that mass is a form of energy, so mass and energy are not separate quantities as the student believes. The special theory of relativity led to this result by showing that a body at rest has energy equal to its mass multiplied by the square of the speed of light, so a body has rest energy simply because it has mass. Mass can therefore act as a store of energy: a small amount of mass corresponds to a very large amount of energy, which is released when mass is converted into other forms of energy in nuclear reactions. This also means that the energy of a body depends on its mass, not only on its motion. The relationship changed the understanding of matter, because it showed that the conservation of mass and energy must be considered together rather than separately.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-mark row: discusses mass as a form of energy and a store of energy, and explains the change in the view of mass and energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: The separate laws describe chemical reactions well, because the energy released or absorbed in a chemical reaction is tiny compared with the mass of the reactants, so any change in mass is far too small to measure. Within that range the laws are a very good approximation, and conservation of energy and conservation of mass can be treated independently in the laboratory. In nuclear reactions, however, the energy changes are large enough to produce a measurable loss of mass, so the separate laws predict the wrong total. The combined law of conservation of mass-energy resolves this, because it treats the mass lost in a nuclear reaction as energy released. The textbook's claim is therefore largely correct, but the failure is one of scope rather than error, since the separate laws remain a valid approximation for chemical reactions. The combined law is needed to describe nuclear reactions consistently and to link the two laws across every type of reaction.

dotPoints.description: Explain the relationship between mass defect and the energy released in a nuclear reaction using E = mc²

prompts.question: Explain the relationship between mass defect and the energy released in a nuclear reaction, using E = mc² to show why a larger mass defect releases more energy.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A student is told that the products of a nuclear reaction have a slightly smaller total mass than the reactants, and asks where the energy released comes from.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass defect is the difference in mass between the reactants and the products of a nuclear reaction, or between separate nucleons and the nucleus they form. This missing mass is converted into energy according to E = mc², so a larger mass defect means more energy released. The energy released is equal to the mass defect multiplied by the square of the speed of light, so the two quantities are directly proportional.

prompts.question: Analyse how the mass defect of a nuclear reaction determines the energy released, and where that energy appears.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: In one reaction, the products have a total mass less than the reactants, and the products move apart at high speed after the reaction.

sampleAnswers.answer: The mass defect of the reaction is the difference between the total mass of the reactants and the total mass of the products, so a positive mass defect means the reaction releases energy. Applying E = mc², this mass defect is converted into energy, so the energy released is proportional to the mass defect. A larger mass defect therefore produces more energy released in the nuclear reaction. This energy does not disappear: it appears as the kinetic energy of the products, which move apart at high speed, and as the energy of any gamma ray photons emitted. This is why the energy released is detected through the motion of the products and the radiation they give off, not through any visible loss of material.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large nucleus. When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, the extra energy makes it unstable, and electrostatic repulsion between its protons overcomes the strong nuclear force holding it together. It splits into two smaller nuclei, the fission products, and releases two or three neutrons and energy, mostly as kinetic energy of the fission products. These neutrons can cause further fission.

prompts.question: Discuss why nuclear fission is used as an energy source, and why the fission products create radioactive waste that must be managed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear fission is a useful energy source because a small mass of uranium-235 releases a very large amount of energy, and the power station produces no carbon dioxide while the reaction is running. The energy is released as kinetic energy of the fission products and as radiation, which heats water to drive turbines, so a controlled fission reaction gives a reliable and continuous supply. However, the fission products are radioactive and remain so for long periods, creating radioactive waste that must be stored and isolated safely. Managing this waste is costly and raises long-term questions about storage. The usefulness of nuclear fission as an energy source must therefore be weighed against the waste produced by its fission products.

prompts.question: Differentiate between controlled and uncontrolled chain reactions, explaining how the number of fissions changes over time in each case and what this means for the energy output.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A power station keeps the number of fissions steady, while a laboratory experiment allows the number of fissions to increase rapidly from one generation to the next.
prompts.markingCriteria:

sampleAnswers.answer: A controlled chain reaction is one in which the number of fissions per generation is kept steady, so on average each fission causes exactly one further fission. The energy output is therefore constant over time, which is how a power reactor operates, with control rods absorbing neutrons to hold the chain reaction at the desired rate. An uncontrolled chain reaction occurs when, on average, more than one neutron from each fission causes a further fission, so the number of fissions per generation increases rapidly. The energy output therefore rises very quickly, and the energy is released in a very short time rather than steadily. The two types differ in whether the number of fissions is held steady or allowed to grow, and this determines whether the energy output is steady or rising.

The coolant carries the heat away from the fuel to produce steam or transfer energy, preventing the fuel from overheating. Together these components allow the fission reactor to keep a steady power output: the moderator sustains the chain reaction, the control rods regulate it, and the coolant removes its heat.

sampleAnswers.answer: The chemical identification of barium was the first stage: Hahn and Strassmann found that bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium, which showed that the uranium nucleus had split. Their contribution was experimental, because the barium was an unexpected product that proved a split had occurred. This explanation gave the earlier result its meaning, so the chemical and physical contributions together established nuclear fission as a process. The first controlled chain reaction, built by Fermi and his team in 1942, then showed that fission could be sustained in a controlled way. Each stage depended on the one before, so the work of these scientists moved fission from an unexpected observation to a usable source of energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Balanced nuclear equations for fusion and fission show that mass number and atomic number are conserved, because the totals on each side of each equation are equal. In a fusion equation, the nuclei on the left join to form a larger nucleus, and the equation shows which nuclei are involved and which products are formed. In a fission equation, a large nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits, and the equation shows the two smaller fission products and any neutrons released. However, the equations do not show the energy released, which depends on the mass difference between the reactants and the products. The student's conclusion is therefore incorrect: the balance of mass number and atomic number says nothing about energy, which must be found from the mass defect.

sampleAnswers.answer: Balanced fusion and fission equations show that mass number and atomic number are conserved.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 2-mark row: describes what the equations show with limited reference to what they omit.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear equations show which nuclei react.

dotPoints.description: Explain why fusion requires high temperatures and pressures

prompts.question: Explain why fusion requires high temperatures and pressures, in terms of the electrostatic repulsion between nuclei and the short range of the strong nuclear force.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A physics class is asked to explain why the Sun's core must be extremely hot and dense before fusion can begin.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains that electrostatic repulsion must be overcome by the high kinetic energy given by high temperatures, and that high pressures bring nuclei within the range of the strong nuclear force
2 marks: Explains that nuclei repel one another, so high temperatures and pressures are needed, with limited reference to the strong nuclear force

markerNotes: Name the repulsion first, since it is the barrier the nuclei must overcome.
Link high temperature to kinetic energy and pressure to closer approach, rather than treating either one alone.

commonStudentErrors: Says high temperatures are needed only to melt the nuclei, rather than to give them kinetic energy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Fusion requires high temperatures and pressures because the nuclei are positively charged, so electrostatic repulsion pushes them apart. High temperatures give the nuclei enough kinetic energy to approach closely, and high pressures bring them together more often. Only at very close range can the short-range strong nuclear force overcome the repulsion and bind the nuclei together.

sampleAnswers.answer: The nuclei repel each other, so high temperatures and pressures are needed to bring them together.

prompts.question: Discuss the difficulty of achieving controlled fusion on Earth, given the high temperatures and pressures that fusion requires.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A research team proposes building a fusion power station on Earth and must decide how to contain the fuel.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the difficulty of controlled fusion in terms of the temperatures and pressures needed, the containment of plasma and the need for a net energy gain, with a justified judgement on the challenge
5 marks: Discusses the high temperatures and pressures needed on Earth and at least one containment method, with clear links to the difficulty
4 marks: Explains why the temperatures and pressures needed for fusion are hard to reproduce on Earth, with some reference to containment
3 marks: Describes the need for high temperatures and pressures in controlled fusion, with limited discussion of difficulty
2 marks: Identifies that controlled fusion requires high temperatures and pressures
1 mark: Provides a minimal relevant response about fusion on Earth
markerNotes: Address both temperature and pressure, and explain why each is hard to achieve on Earth.
Name a containment method, such as magnetic or inertial confinement, and say why it is needed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Controlled fusion on Earth is difficult because the fuel must be heated to temperatures far above those at the centre of the Sun, since the Sun's core relies on enormous gravitational pressure that cannot be reproduced on Earth. At these temperatures the fuel is a plasma, which would melt or vaporise any solid container. Researchers therefore use magnetic confinement, in which strong magnetic fields hold the charged plasma away from the walls, or inertial confinement, in which lasers compress a small fuel pellet to high pressures for a brief moment. Both methods must achieve high temperatures and pressures together for long enough that more energy is released than was put in, a condition that remains difficult to sustain in practice. The difficulty is therefore one of engineering as well as physics: the fusion reaction is understood, but sustaining the conditions in a stable and controlled way remains the central challenge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 6-mark row: discusses temperature, pressure and containment, and gives a balanced judgement on the difficulty.

dotPoints.description: Compare the energy release of nuclear reactions with the energy release of fossil fuels and conventional explosives

prompts.question: Describe how the energy release of nuclear reactions compares with that of fossil fuels and conventional explosives, per unit mass of fuel.

markerNotes: Compare on the same basis, energy per unit mass of fuel, so that the comparison is fair.
Explain the reason: chemical reactions change only the arrangement of electrons, while nuclear reactions change the nucleus.

States that nuclear reactions release less energy than explosives, because nuclear fuel is rare.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear reactions release vastly more energy per unit mass of fuel than fossil fuels or conventional explosives. Burning fossil fuels and detonating conventional explosives are chemical reactions that rearrange electrons, whereas a nuclear reaction changes the nucleus itself, so its energy release is far larger.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-mark row: compares both comparators per unit mass and explains the nuclear origin of the larger release.

sampleAnswers.answer: Nuclear reactions release much more energy per unit mass than fossil fuels, which are burned in chemical reactions.
